disease.name: Hypothyroidism
disease.scientific_name: Hypothyroidism / Thyroid Hormone Deficiency / Underactive Thyroid
disease.icd_10_code: E03.9 (Hypothyroidism, unspecified); E03.0 (Congenital hypothyroidism with diffuse goitre); E03.1 (Congenital hypothyroidism without goitre); E02 (Subclinical iodine-deficiency hypothyroidism); E00 (Congenital iodine-deficiency syndrome / Cretinism); E06.3 (Autoimmune thyroiditis — Hashimoto's disease); E89.0 (Post-procedural hypothyroidism); E23.0 (Secondary hypothyroidism — pituitary); P72.2 (Transitory neonatal hypothyroidism)
disease.category: Endocrine Disease / Metabolic Disorder / Autoimmune Disease

overview.description: Hypothyroidism is a common endocrine disorder in which the thyroid gland — a butterfly-shaped gland at the base of the neck — fails to produce sufficient thyroid hormones (primarily thyroxine / T4 and triiodothyronine / T3) to meet the body's metabolic requirements. Thyroid hormones are essential regulators of virtually every organ system: they control basal metabolic rate, energy production, body temperature, heart rate, growth, neurological development, reproductive function, and the metabolism of carbohydrates, proteins, and lipids. A deficiency produces a progressive slowing of all body functions — manifesting as fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, depression, bradycardia, and cognitive impairment — and can progress to life-threatening complications including myxoedema coma if untreated. Hypothyroidism is highly treatable with once-daily oral thyroid hormone replacement therapy and most patients achieve complete symptom resolution with correct management.
overview.affected_organ: Primarily the thyroid gland; systemically affects virtually all organ systems — cardiovascular, neurological, musculoskeletal, reproductive, gastrointestinal, dermatological, and metabolic
overview.prevalence: Overt hypothyroidism affects 1-2% of the general population globally; subclinical hypothyroidism (elevated TSH, normal Free T4) affects 4-10% of adults; approximately 200 million people worldwide have some form of thyroid disease; iodine deficiency affects 1.9 billion people and is the most common preventable cause of thyroid dysfunction globally
overview.age_group: All ages; most common in women over 40 years; prevalence increases progressively with age; peak incidence in women aged 40-60 years; congenital form present from birth
overview.is_contagious_note: Hypothyroidism is not infectious or contagious; the autoimmune form (Hashimoto's) has genetic predisposition and may cluster in families
overview.is_curable_note: Most forms are lifelong conditions requiring ongoing treatment; however, some transient causes (postpartum thyroiditis, drug-induced, subacute thyroiditis) can resolve completely. Congenital hypothyroidism and post-surgical/radioiodine forms are permanent.
overview.is_preventable_note: Iodine-deficiency hypothyroidism is entirely preventable through universal salt iodisation; neonatal screening prevents intellectual disability from congenital hypothyroidism; drug-induced forms preventable through monitoring
overview.key_fact: Hypothyroidism is one of the most commonly missed diagnoses — symptoms are non-specific, gradual, and often attributed to normal ageing or other conditions; a simple TSH blood test can diagnose or exclude it

types.name: Primary Hypothyroidism
types.description: The most common form — accounting for over 95% of all hypothyroidism. The thyroid gland itself is dysfunctional, failing to produce adequate T4 and T3. As serum T4 falls, the pituitary responds by increasing TSH secretion (negative feedback); therefore TSH is ELEVATED and Free T4 is LOW in primary hypothyroidism. It includes multiple aetiologies, all converging on the same thyroid gland failure.

subtypes.subtype: Autoimmune Thyroiditis — Hashimoto's Thyroiditis (Chronic Lymphocytic Thyroiditis)
subtypes.description: The most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient countries (Europe, North America, urban India). An autoimmune process in which autoreactive T-lymphocytes infiltrate the thyroid gland and autoantibodies (anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin) progressively destroy thyroid follicular cells, leading to glandular atrophy and failure of hormone production over years to decades.
subtypes.epidemiology: Affects 2% of women and 0.2% of men; female-to-male ratio 7-10:1; peak onset 40-60 years but can occur at any age including children
subtypes.markers: Elevated anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies (anti-TPO Ab) — present in >90% of cases; elevated anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (anti-Tg Ab) — present in ~60%; thyroid ultrasound: heterogeneous, hypoechoic parenchyma with reduced vascularity
subtypes.natural_history: May pass through an initial transient hyperthyroid phase (Hashitoxicosis) due to follicle destruction releasing stored hormone, then becomes euthyroid, then progresses to hypothyroidism over years; 2-5% annual conversion rate from subclinical to overt hypothyroidism when anti-TPO positive
subtypes.associations: Associated with other autoimmune conditions: Type 1 diabetes, Addison's disease, vitiligo, pernicious anaemia, coeliac disease, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren's syndrome (autoimmune polyglandular syndrome)

subtypes.description: The most common cause of hypothyroidism and goitre GLOBALLY — particularly in low-income countries in Africa, Southeast Asia, South America, and Central Asia. Iodine is an essential raw material for thyroid hormone synthesis; without it, the thyroid cannot produce T3 or T4. Chronic iodine deficiency leads to goitre (thyroid gland enlargement as it attempts to compensate) and eventually frank hypothyroidism.
subtypes.epidemiology: Affects approximately 740 million people globally; 50 million have overt thyroid disease from iodine deficiency; a public health priority in landlocked countries and mountainous regions where soil and water have low iodine content
subtypes.markers: Low urinary iodine concentration (<100 mcg/L indicates deficiency); elevated TSH; enlarged thyroid (goitre); normal or low anti-TPO antibodies (not autoimmune)
subtypes.prevention: Universal salt iodisation (USI) — adding 20-40 parts per million iodine to table salt — the single most cost-effective public health nutrition intervention; mandatory in India under FSSAI regulations
subtypes.note: Paradoxically, excessive iodine intake (e.g., from amiodarone, contrast dyes, kelp supplements) can also cause hypothyroidism (Wolff-Chaikoff effect)

subtypes.description: Permanent hypothyroidism following total thyroidectomy (complete removal of thyroid gland) or subtotal thyroidectomy. Expected and inevitable after total thyroidectomy — all patients require lifelong levothyroxine replacement. After subtotal/partial thyroidectomy — risk depends on remnant tissue left.
subtypes.indications_for_thyroidectomy: Thyroid cancer, large goitre causing compressive symptoms, Grave's disease (hyperthyroidism), toxic nodules
subtypes.onset: Hypothyroidism typically develops within 4-6 weeks of total thyroidectomy
subtypes.management: Levothyroxine started immediately postoperatively after total thyroidectomy — dose 1.6 mcg/kg/day; for cancer patients suppressive therapy (TSH <0.1) may be targeted initially

subtypes.description: Hypothyroidism is a predictable and often intended consequence of radioactive iodine-131 (I-131) therapy for hyperthyroidism (Grave's disease, toxic multinodular goitre, toxic adenoma) or thyroid cancer ablation. The radioiodine selectively destroys thyroid follicular cells.
subtypes.onset: Hypothyroidism usually develops 2-6 months after RAI therapy; risk increases progressively over years
subtypes.management: TSH monitoring at 4-6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, then annually; lifelong levothyroxine once hypothyroidism confirmed

subtypes.description: Several commonly prescribed medications interfere with thyroid hormone synthesis, secretion, or peripheral metabolism, causing hypothyroidism. Drug-induced hypothyroidism is often overlooked as a medication side effect.

causative_drugs.mechanism: High iodine content (37% iodine by weight) — inhibits T4-to-T3 conversion; Wolff-Chaikoff effect; direct thyroid cytotoxicity. Also can cause hyperthyroidism.
causative_drugs.risk: Hypothyroidism in 15-22% of patients on amiodarone; higher risk in iodine-sufficient areas; MONITOR TSH every 6 months in all patients on amiodarone

causative_drugs.mechanism: Blocks thyroid hormone synthesis and secretion; inhibits proteolysis of thyroglobulin; enhances autoimmune thyroid destruction
causative_drugs.risk: Goitre in 40-50% of long-term lithium users; hypothyroidism in 20-40%; MONITOR TSH every 6-12 months

causative_drugs.mechanism: Intended inhibition of thyroid peroxidase for hyperthyroidism treatment — dose-dependent hypothyroidism if overtreated
causative_drugs.note: Reversible on dose reduction; requires careful TSH monitoring

causative_drugs.mechanism: Triggers autoimmune thyroiditis by activating autoreactive lymphocytes
causative_drugs.risk: Hypothyroidism in 5-10% of patients; typically reversible after stopping treatment

causative_drugs.mechanism: Immune system activation causes autoimmune thyroiditis (immune-related adverse event — irAE)
causative_drugs.risk: Hypothyroidism in 5-20% of cancer patients on checkpoint inhibitors; often permanent; screen TSH before each cycle

causative_drugs.mechanism: Direct thyroid cell destruction; reduced T4 absorption; impaired TSH-stimulated thyroid growth
causative_drugs.risk: Hypothyroidism in 36-85% of patients on sunitinib
Monitor TSH in patients on these agents

subtypes.description: Autoimmune thyroid inflammation occurring within 12 months of delivery, miscarriage, or termination of pregnancy. The rebound of immune function after the immunosuppressive state of pregnancy triggers autoimmune thyroid inflammation.
subtypes.phases: Classic triphasic: (1) Hyperthyroid phase (1-4 months postpartum) — painless, brief; (2) Hypothyroid phase (4-8 months) — fatigue, depression, cold intolerance — often mistaken for postnatal depression; (3) Recovery phase (most return to euthyroid by 12 months, but 30-50% develop permanent hypothyroidism within 5-10 years)
subtypes.epidemiology: Affects 5-10% of women after delivery; 50% have positive anti-TPO antibodies
subtypes.diagnosis: TSH, Free T4, anti-TPO antibodies; thyroid scan shows decreased uptake (distinguishes from Grave's hyperthyroid phase)
subtypes.management: Hypothyroid phase: levothyroxine if symptomatic or TSH >10; wean off at 12 months to assess permanent status; long-term annual TSH monitoring

subtypes.description: Uncommon causes in which infiltration of the thyroid gland by abnormal cells or substances destroys functional thyroid tissue.
examples: Riedel's thyroiditis — fibrous replacement of thyroid tissue; presents as hard 'woody' goitre; associated with other fibrosclerotic diseases
Haemochromatosis — iron deposition in thyroid gland
Thyroid lymphoma — usually on background of Hashimoto's; rapidly enlarging goitre

types.name: Central Hypothyroidism (Secondary and Tertiary)
types.description: Rare form (less than 1% of hypothyroidism) in which the defect lies not in the thyroid gland itself but in the hypothalamus or pituitary gland — resulting in inadequate TSH stimulation of an otherwise normal thyroid. TSH is LOW or inappropriately normal (pituitary fails to raise TSH despite low T4). Distinguishing feature: TSH is not elevated, unlike primary hypothyroidism.

subtypes.description: Deficiency of TSH from pituitary gland damage — part of hypopituitarism. Causes include: pituitary adenoma and its treatment (surgery/radiotherapy), Sheehan's syndrome (postpartum pituitary necrosis from haemorrhage), traumatic brain injury, pituitary apoplexy, infiltration (sarcoidosis, haemochromatosis, lymphoma), empty sella syndrome.
subtypes.diagnosis: Low or normal TSH with low Free T4; MRI pituitary (sellar lesion); assessment of other pituitary hormones (growth hormone, cortisol, FSH/LH, prolactin); dynamic pituitary testing if needed
subtypes.management: Treat underlying pituitary disease; levothyroxine replacement; CRITICAL: ALWAYS replace cortisol (hydrocortisone) BEFORE starting levothyroxine in hypopituitarism to prevent precipitating adrenal crisis

subtypes.description: Deficiency of thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) from hypothalamic damage — TRH normally stimulates pituitary TSH secretion. Causes: craniopharyngioma, hypothalamic tumours, infiltration, head trauma, cranial irradiation.
subtypes.diagnosis: Low TSH, low Free T4; TRH stimulation test; MRI hypothalamus/pituitary
subtypes.note: Central hypothyroidism from hypothalamic or pituitary disease often co-exists with deficiencies of other pituitary hormones (growth hormone, ACTH, FSH/LH, ADH) requiring complete pituitary hormone assessment

types.name: Subclinical Hypothyroidism
types.description: A biochemical diagnosis — elevated serum TSH (typically 4.5-10 mIU/L) with a normal Free T4 level. Patients may be entirely asymptomatic or have very mild, non-specific symptoms. Subclinical hypothyroidism is not a minor condition — it carries significant long-term implications for cardiovascular health, lipid metabolism, cognition, and fertility. Management is individualised based on TSH level, symptoms, anti-TPO status, cardiovascular risk, and patient age.
types.epidemiology: Affects 4-10% of adults; prevalence increases to 20% in women over 60 years; the most common thyroid abnormality found on routine health screening
types.natural_history: Without treatment: 2-5% per year progress to overt hypothyroidism; higher progression rate if anti-TPO antibodies positive (7-10% per year) or TSH >10 mIU/L
treatment_indications: TSH >10 mIU/L — most guidelines recommend treatment regardless of symptoms
TSH 4.5-10 mIU/L with positive anti-TPO antibodies — consider treatment
TSH 4.5-10 mIU/L with symptoms of hypothyroidism — consider treatment
Pregnancy or planning pregnancy — treat if TSH >2.5 mIU/L
Infertility or recurrent miscarriage — treat if TSH >2.5 mIU/L
Dyslipidaemia or cardiovascular risk — treat if TSH >7-10 mIU/L
Age >70 years with TSH mildly elevated — evidence for treatment benefit is less clear; avoid over-treatment

types.name: Congenital Hypothyroidism
types.description: Hypothyroidism present from birth due to absence, underdevelopment, or malfunction of the thyroid gland. The most common preventable cause of intellectual disability worldwide. Neonatal screening (Guthrie/heel-prick test) has transformed outcomes — early treatment prevents irreversible brain damage. Without screening and treatment within the first 2 weeks of life, congenital hypothyroidism causes cretinism — severe intellectual disability, short stature, and developmental delay.
types.incidence: 1 in 2,000-4,000 live births; more common in Down syndrome (1 in 100)
causes: Thyroid dysgenesis (75-80%): agenesis (no thyroid), hypoplasia (small thyroid), ectopic thyroid (lingual thyroid most common — at base of tongue)
Dyshormonogenesis (10-15%): normal thyroid location but defective enzyme pathways for hormone synthesis — autosomal recessive; associated with goitre
Transient congenital hypothyroidism: maternal anti-thyroid antibodies crossing placenta (passive transfer); maternal anti-thyroid drug use; neonatal iodine exposure/deficiency
Central congenital hypothyroidism: TSH deficiency from pituitary (rare)
signs_in_neonate: Prolonged neonatal jaundice (beyond 2 weeks) — most common presenting sign
Large anterior fontanelle (delayed closure) with wide sutures
types.screening: Heel-prick blood test (Guthrie test) at 5-7 days of life measuring TSH (and T4 in some programmes); TSH >40 mIU/L on screening is diagnostic; universal neonatal thyroid screening now standard in 57+ countries including India (increasingly implemented)
types.treatment: IV or oral levothyroxine started within first 2 weeks of life — initial dose 10-15 mcg/kg/day; TSH target <5 mIU/L in first year; Free T4 maintained in upper half of normal range; lifelong treatment in permanent forms
types.prognosis: Excellent neurodevelopmental outcome with early (within 2 weeks) and adequate treatment; delayed treatment results in irreversible intellectual impairment proportional to duration of untreated hypothyroidism

types.name: Transient Hypothyroidism
types.description: Hypothyroidism that is temporary and expected to resolve spontaneously or after removal of the cause. Important to recognise to avoid committing patients to unnecessary lifelong treatment.
causes: Subacute (De Quervain's) thyroiditis: post-viral painful thyroid inflammation — initial hyperthyroid phase from follicle rupture, then hypothyroid phase as stores depleted, then recovery; 90% return to euthyroid
Silent thyroiditis (painless sporadic thyroiditis): similar triphasic pattern to postpartum thyroiditis but not pregnancy-related
Postpartum thyroiditis hypothyroid phase: often transient; reassess at 12 months
Drug-induced hypothyroidism: from interferon-alpha, checkpoint inhibitors — may resolve after drug cessation
Neonatal hypothyroidism from maternal anti-thyroid drugs or antibodies
Excessive iodine load (contrast media, amiodarone in iodine-deficient patients) — Wolff-Chaikoff effect: usually transient as thyroid escapes from iodine excess
types.management: Treat if symptomatic with levothyroxine; attempt withdrawal at 6-12 months (reduce dose by 50%, recheck TSH in 4-6 weeks); label as transient to ensure periodic reassessment rather than automatic lifelong prescription

severity_levels.name: Subclinical Hypothyroidism
severity_levels.description: Biochemical elevation of TSH with normal Free T4 and absent or very mild symptoms. Thyroid hormone deficiency is compensated by the elevated TSH drive.
severity_levels.tsh_range: TSH 4.5-10 mIU/L (mild subclinical); TSH >10 mIU/L (moderate subclinical)
severity_levels.symptoms: Often asymptomatic; vague non-specific fatigue or mild weight gain may be present; difficult to attribute symptoms to thyroid specifically
severity_levels.functional_impact: Minimal; most activities unaffected; quality of life impact variable
severity_levels.management: Individualised — see treatment indications. Annual TSH monitoring. Levothyroxine for TSH >10, pregnancy, anti-TPO positive, or symptomatic. Lifestyle optimisation (iodine, selenium, stress).
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Rise in TSH to >10 mIU/L; development of overt symptoms; positive anti-TPO antibodies; planning pregnancy

severity_levels.name: Mild Overt Hypothyroidism
severity_levels.description: Low Free T4 with elevated TSH and a constellation of mild symptoms that noticeably affect quality of life. Diagnosis is biochemically confirmed.
severity_levels.free_t4: Low (below lower limit of reference range)
severity_levels.symptoms: Fatigue and low energy; mild weight gain; cold intolerance; constipation; dry skin; mild depression or low mood; slight bradycardia; mild dyslipidaemia on blood tests
severity_levels.functional_impact: Reduced energy and concentration affecting work performance; exercise tolerance reduced; social withdrawal from fatigue
severity_levels.management: Levothyroxine oral replacement; starting dose 50-75 mcg/day in otherwise healthy adults under 60 (lower if elderly or cardiac history); TSH recheck at 4-8 weeks; titrate to TSH target 0.5-2.5 mIU/L
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Worsening symptoms; TSH >50 mIU/L; cardiovascular or neurological involvement

severity_levels.name: Moderate to Severe Overt Hypothyroidism
severity_levels.description: Markedly elevated TSH with significantly low Free T4 and prominent multi-system symptoms substantially impairing daily function. Requires prompt treatment.
severity_levels.symptoms: Profound fatigue; significant unexplained weight gain; severe cold intolerance; constipation; periorbital and peripheral non-pitting oedema (myxoedema); coarsened skin; hair thinning/loss; hoarse voice; bradycardia; hypertension (diastolic); hyperlipidaemia; depression; cognitive slowing; menstrual disturbances; impotence; carpal tunnel syndrome; muscle aches and weakness; delayed deep tendon reflexes (hung-up reflexes); pericardial or pleural effusion; macroglossia
severity_levels.functional_impact: Significantly impairs work, exercise, relationships, and daily activities; high risk of cardiovascular complications and reproductive failure
severity_levels.management: Levothyroxine — start at appropriate dose; elderly/cardiac patients start at 12.5-25 mcg; refer to endocrinology; monitor for improvement; check for precipitants or complications; add T3 if refractory. Evaluate for associated autoimmune conditions.
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Altered consciousness; hypothermia; cardiovascular instability — MYXOEDEMA COMA

severity_levels.name: Myxoedema Coma — Critical / Life-Threatening
severity_levels.description: The most severe and life-threatening manifestation of untreated or undertreated hypothyroidism. Myxoedema coma is a medical emergency with a mortality rate of 20-60% even with optimal treatment. It represents the extreme end of hypothyroid decompensation — precipitated by a stressor in a patient with longstanding severe hypothyroidism.
severity_levels.precipitating_factors: Cold exposure (most common precipitant in elderly); infection (pneumonia, sepsis, UTI); myocardial infarction; stroke; trauma; major surgery; sedatives, opioids, or anaesthetic agents; hypoglycaemia; hypoxia; medication non-compliance; GI bleeding
clinical_features: Altered consciousness — stupor, obtundation, or frank coma
Hypothermia — core body temperature <35°C (often <32°C) — cardinal feature
Hypoventilation — CO2 retention; hypoxia; risk of respiratory arrest
severity_levels.management: ICU admission; IV levothyroxine 200-400 mcg IV bolus then 50-100 mcg IV daily; IV T3 (liothyronine) 5-20 mcg initially if T4-to-T3 conversion impaired; IV hydrocortisone 100 mg every 8 hours (adrenal insufficiency must always be presumed); passive rewarming; IV fluids cautiously (hyponatraemia risk); mechanical ventilation if hypoventilating; treat precipitating cause; continuous cardiac monitoring
severity_levels.mortality: 20-60% even with aggressive treatment; mortality increases with severity of hypothermia, coma depth, and delayed presentation; best outcomes with early diagnosis and aggressive ICU management

causative_mechanisms_overview.autoimmune: Most common cause in iodine-sufficient countries — Hashimoto's thyroiditis accounts for 70-80% of primary hypothyroidism in developed nations; anti-TPO antibodies mark autoimmune thyroid destruction
causative_mechanisms_overview.iodine_deficiency: Most common cause globally — responsible for the majority of hypothyroidism and goitre in low-income countries; preventable with universal salt iodisation
causative_mechanisms_overview.iatrogenic: Post-thyroidectomy and post-radioiodine therapy are predictable and common causes in clinical practice
causative_mechanisms_overview.drug_induced: Amiodarone, lithium, and immune checkpoint inhibitors are the most clinically important drug causes; increasingly common with expanding cancer immunotherapy use
causative_mechanisms_overview.central: Pituitary or hypothalamic disease — rare but important as TSH is not elevated; requires different diagnostic and therapeutic approach
causative_mechanisms_overview.congenital: Thyroid agenesis or dyshormonogenesis — screened at birth in most countries

pathophysiology.normal_thyroid_axis: Hypothalamus secretes thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH) → stimulates pituitary to release TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) → TSH binds to receptors on thyroid follicular cells → thyroid synthesises T4 (thyroxine — major product) and T3 (triiodothyronine — active form) → T4 released into blood, converted peripherally to active T3 by deiodinase enzymes in liver, kidney, and other tissues → T3 enters cells, binds nuclear thyroid hormone receptors, regulates gene transcription → negative feedback: T3/T4 suppress TRH and TSH
pathophysiology.thyroid_hormone_synthesis: Iodine (from diet) is actively transported into thyroid follicular cells → organified (bound to thyroglobulin) by thyroid peroxidase (TPO) → MIT (monoiodotyrosine) and DIT (diiodotyrosine) are coupled to form T3 (MIT+DIT) and T4 (DIT+DIT) → stored as thyroglobulin colloid in follicles → released on TSH stimulation
pathophysiology.peripheral_conversion: Approximately 80% of circulating T3 is derived from peripheral deiodination of T4 by selenoenzyme deiodinases (selenium-dependent); only 20% directly secreted by thyroid. This is why selenium deficiency can impair thyroid function even with adequate iodine.
pathophysiology.deficiency_consequences: Without adequate T3: nuclear receptors are unoccupied → reduced gene transcription → slowed protein synthesis → reduced Na+/K+ ATPase activity (lower heat production) → slowed carbohydrate and lipid metabolism → reduced cardiac contractility and heart rate → impaired neuronal function and myelination → reduced gut motility → impaired growth hormone signalling

risk_factors: Female sex — 7-10 times higher risk than men
Age over 40 years — prevalence increases steadily with age
Personal or family history of autoimmune thyroid disease or other autoimmune conditions (Type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, Addison's disease, vitiligo, coeliac disease, pernicious anaemia)
Positive anti-TPO antibody titres — 7-10% annual progression to overt hypothyroidism
Down syndrome (Trisomy 21) — 15-20% lifetime risk of hypothyroidism
Turner syndrome — 10-30% prevalence of autoimmune thyroiditis
Previous thyroid surgery or radioiodine therapy
Current or previous treatment with amiodarone, lithium, interferon-alpha, or checkpoint inhibitors
Residing in iodine-deficient area (landlocked regions, mountainous areas, areas without salt iodisation)
Excessive iodine consumption — high seaweed/kelp intake, iodine supplements, iodinated contrast media
Previous head and neck irradiation (for lymphoma, nasopharyngeal cancer)
Pregnancy and postpartum period — risk of autoimmune thyroiditis increased
Previous postpartum thyroiditis — 50% risk of permanent hypothyroidism within 5-10 years
Obesity — associated with higher TSH levels (cause vs effect unclear)
Smoking — paradoxically appears to reduce risk of hypothyroidism (thiocyanates may have mild stimulatory effect) but increases risk of Grave's ophthalmopathy
Chronic stress — HPA axis activation suppresses thyroid function
Selenium deficiency — impairs T4-to-T3 conversion and reduces antioxidant protection of thyroid
Gut microbiome dysbiosis — emerging evidence of gut-thyroid axis; impaired iodine and selenium absorption

symptoms.overview: Symptoms of hypothyroidism are notoriously non-specific, insidious in onset, and often overlap with depression, anaemia, chronic fatigue syndrome, and normal ageing. Many patients are diagnosed on routine blood testing rather than from specific complaints. The severity of symptoms correlates imperfectly with biochemical severity — some patients have TSH >100 mIU/L with minimal symptoms; others with TSH 10 mIU/L are significantly debilitated. Symptom onset is gradual (months to years) and patients often adapt unknowingly.

primary_symptoms.name: Fatigue and Low Energy
primary_symptoms.description: The most common and prominent symptom — present in over 90% of patients with overt hypothyroidism. Characterised by profound, persistent tiredness not relieved by sleep; lack of energy for daily activities; reduced motivation and drive. Thyroid hormone is essential for mitochondrial energy production — deficiency reduces ATP generation in all cells. The fatigue of hypothyroidism is typically worse in the morning (unlike fibromyalgia) and improves through the day.
primary_symptoms.onset: Insidious — develops over months to years

primary_symptoms.name: Weight Gain
primary_symptoms.description: Unexplained weight gain despite no change in diet or activity — typically 3-10 kg; rarely more than 10-15 kg from hypothyroidism alone. Caused by: reduced basal metabolic rate (BMR), fluid retention (myxoedema), reduced physical activity from fatigue, and lipid accumulation. Patients with hypothyroidism rarely gain very large amounts of weight from thyroid deficiency alone — significant obesity should prompt evaluation for other causes.
primary_symptoms.note: Weight gain is NOT the most reliable or specific symptom — most overweight individuals do NOT have hypothyroidism. However, unexplained weight gain with other features warrants TSH testing.

primary_symptoms.name: Cold Intolerance
primary_symptoms.description: Feeling excessively cold compared to others in the same environment — peripheral vasoconstriction and reduced thermogenesis from low thyroid hormone. Patients often need extra clothing, blankets, or heating when others are comfortable. Hypothermia (low core body temperature) is the extreme form seen in myxoedema coma.
primary_symptoms.onset: Gradual — often noticed in comparison with others

primary_symptoms.name: Constipation
primary_symptoms.description: Slowing of gastrointestinal motility from reduced thyroid-mediated stimulation of gut smooth muscle and reduced prostaglandin synthesis. Reduced transit time leads to hard, infrequent stools. Severe constipation can cause faecal impaction and rarely ileus (paralytic ileus in myxoedema coma).
primary_symptoms.onset: Gradual — often not attributed to thyroid disease

primary_symptoms.name: Dry Skin and Hair Changes
primary_symptoms.description: Reduced sebaceous and sweat gland secretion causing dry, rough, scaly skin (xerosis); skin may appear sallow or yellow-tinged (carotenaemia — impaired conversion of beta-carotene to Vitamin A). Hair becomes dry, brittle, coarse, and may fall out diffusely (telogen effluvium); outer third of eyebrows may be lost (Queen Anne's sign — lateral eyebrow loss, a classical clinical sign). Nails become brittle and grow slowly.

primary_symptoms.name: Bradycardia and Cardiovascular Changes
primary_symptoms.description: Reduced heart rate (bradycardia — often <60 bpm) from reduced sympathetic sensitivity and reduced cardiac myosin ATPase activity. Reduced cardiac output and stroke volume. Diastolic hypertension is common (peripheral vasoconstriction despite low cardiac output). Pericardial effusion occurs in 25-35% of patients with overt hypothyroidism (usually small and haemodynamically insignificant). ECG changes: low voltage, prolonged QT interval, flattened/inverted T waves.
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild to Moderate (rarely severe unless in myxoedema coma)
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Dyslipidaemia is a major consequence — elevated total cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol, and triglycerides, increasing long-term cardiovascular risk

primary_symptoms.name: Oedema (Non-pitting / Myxoedema)
primary_symptoms.description: Accumulation of glycosaminoglycans (hyaluronic acid and chondroitin sulphate) in skin and subcutaneous tissues — this creates a characteristic non-pitting (does not pit on sustained finger pressure, unlike cardiac or renal oedema) puffy appearance. Typically affects: face (periorbital puffiness — classic), hands, feet, and tongue (macroglossia). The term 'myxoedema' refers to this mucous (myx-) oedema — it is pathognomonic of severe untreated hypothyroidism.
primary_symptoms.onset: Gradual — correlates with duration and severity of hypothyroidism

primary_symptoms.name: Neurological and Cognitive Symptoms
primary_symptoms.description: Thyroid hormone is essential for neuronal myelination, synaptic transmission, and cerebral glucose metabolism. Deficiency causes: cognitive slowing ('brain fog'), impaired concentration and memory, psychomotor slowing, depression (hypothyroidism is a reversible cause of depression — all new depression should have TSH checked), and occasionally frank dementia (reversible with treatment). Cerebellar ataxia, peripheral neuropathy (with numbness and tingling — carpal tunnel syndrome very common), and in severe cases psychosis (myxoedema madness).

primary_symptoms.name: Menstrual Irregularities and Reproductive Effects
primary_symptoms.description: Hypothyroidism disrupts the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. In women: menorrhagia (heavy periods) is classic; anovulation and oligomenorrhoea; infertility; recurrent miscarriage; hyperprolactinaemia (elevated prolactin from elevated TRH stimulating prolactin as well as TSH) causing galactorrhoea and further menstrual disruption. In men: reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, reduced sperm count and motility. Both sexes: impaired gonadotropin release.
primary_symptoms.severity: Mild to Severe — major cause of treatable infertility
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: All women with unexplained menorrhagia, infertility, or recurrent miscarriage should have TSH measured

primary_symptoms.name: Hoarse Voice
primary_symptoms.description: Myxoedematous infiltration of the laryngeal mucosa and vocal cords causes characteristic low-pitched, husky, hoarse voice quality. Combined with macroglossia and pharyngeal oedema, this can also cause obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA), snoring, and nocturnal breathing problems — an underrecognised cause of OSA.
primary_symptoms.onset: Gradual — patients often do not notice the change themselves

secondary_symptoms: Muscle weakness and aches (myopathy) — proximal muscle weakness; elevated serum creatine kinase (CK); can mimic polymyositis
Delayed deep tendon reflexes ('hung-up' reflexes) — the classic neurological sign of hypothyroidism; particularly evident at the ankle jerk reflex
Carpal tunnel syndrome — bilateral numbness, tingling, and pain in hands from myxoedematous compression of median nerve in carpal tunnel; often bilateral
Goitre (thyroid gland enlargement) — present in Hashimoto's (firm, rubbery, lobulated) and iodine-deficiency hypothyroidism; not present in atrophic thyroiditis or post-surgical/radioiodine
Depression and anxiety — hypothyroidism is a highly treatable reversible cause; screen TSH in all new cases of depression
Decreased sweating (anhidrosis) — reduced sweat gland activity
Slow speech and movement — psychomotor retardation in severe cases
Hearing loss — myxoedematous infiltration of the middle ear and cochlea
Hyperprolactinaemia — from elevated TRH stimulating prolactin; causes galactorrhoea (milk production outside pregnancy) and worsens menstrual disruption
Elevated creatine kinase (CK) — from myopathy; can be markedly elevated (>1000 U/L) — may raise concern for rhabdomyolysis
Normochromic normocytic anaemia — from reduced erythropoietin stimulation; also B12/folate deficiency (associated autoimmune gastritis); iron-deficiency anaemia from menorrhagia
Sleep disturbances — hypersomnia (excessive sleeping), sleep apnoea, altered sleep architecture
Low libido in both men and women
Yellow/sallow skin tinge (carotenaemia) — impaired hepatic conversion of carotene
Disproportionate elevation of serum LDL-cholesterol and triglycerides — from reduced hepatic LDL receptor expression
Hyponatraemia (low blood sodium) — from inappropriate ADH secretion; can cause confusion
warning_signs_of_severe_disease: Altered level of consciousness — confusion, stupor, or unresponsive — possible myxoedema coma — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES
Core body temperature <35°C (hypothermia) with altered consciousness — myxoedema coma trigger — EMERGENCY
Heart rate consistently below 40-45 bpm with fatigue and swelling — severe bradycardia
Inability to breathe properly, hypoventilation, or CO2 retention — respiratory failure in myxoedema coma
Severe hyponatraemia — sodium <125 mmol/L — seizures, confusion, cerebral oedema risk
New-onset psychosis, severe depression with suicidal ideation, or dementia symptoms — possible severe neuropsychiatric hypothyroidism
Rapidly enlarging goitre with choking, stridor, or dysphagia — possible malignancy or Riedel's thyroiditis — urgent referral
Chest pain, dyspnoea, or very large pericardial effusion — haemodynamic compromise
Paralytic ileus or severe constipation with abdominal distension — possible myxoedema ileus
Myxoedema coma is most commonly precipitated by: infection (especially pneumonia), cold exposure, and sedative/opiate medications in elderly patients with undiagnosed severe hypothyroidism

cardiovascular: ECG: prolonged QTc, low voltage, T-wave changes
neurological: Seizures (in severe hyponatraemia or myxoedema coma)
musculoskeletal: Calf hypertrophy (pseudohypertrophy in children — Kocher-Debre-Semelaigne syndrome)

incubation_onset_guide.description: Unlike infectious diseases, hypothyroidism has a very gradual onset. The rate of symptom development depends on speed of thyroid failure — acute loss (post-surgery) is faster than autoimmune progression.

guide.context: Post-total thyroidectomy — hypothyroidism is expected and develops quickly
Autoimmune Hashimoto's thyroiditis — gradual insidious progression
Iodine deficiency — slow progressive decline with goitre enlargement
Congenital hypothyroidism — signs apparent within days to weeks if not screened

medical_history: Onset, duration, and progression of symptoms — fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, cognitive changes, menstrual irregularities, hair and skin changes
Previous thyroid disease or surgery — thyroidectomy, radioiodine therapy, previous thyroid function tests and results
Neck symptoms — goitre (swelling), pain or tenderness (subacute thyroiditis), rapid enlargement (red flag for malignancy)
Medication history — amiodarone, lithium, immunotherapy agents, anti-thyroid drugs, interferon, tyrosine kinase inhibitors, iodinated contrast, excess iodine supplements
Family history — autoimmune thyroid disease, autoimmune conditions (Type 1 diabetes, pernicious anaemia, Addison's, rheumatoid arthritis, vitiligo, coeliac disease)
Personal autoimmune history — Type 1 diabetes, coeliac disease, Addison's disease, pernicious anaemia, rheumatoid arthritis
Reproductive history — recurrent miscarriage, infertility, menorrhagia, postpartum illness
Geographic history — residence in iodine-deficient region; recent iodine contrast exposure
Dietary history — iodine intake (dairy, seafood, iodised salt); selenium intake; excessive goitrogen consumption; vegan diet (lower iodine)
Pregnancy status or plans — critical for TSH target and levothyroxine dosing decisions
Sleep quality and snoring — sleep apnoea assessment
Mental health history — depression, anxiety (hypothyroidism as reversible cause)
Down syndrome or Turner syndrome — higher risk of autoimmune thyroiditis
Recent viral illness (subacute/De Quervain's thyroiditis), neck pain and tenderness
Symptoms of other pituitary hormone deficiencies (secondary hypothyroidism): galactorrhoea, amenorrhoea, short stature, headache, visual field changes
physical_examination: Vital signs: heart rate (bradycardia <60 bpm), blood pressure (diastolic hypertension), temperature (hypothermia in severe disease), weight and BMI (compare with previous if available)

Thyroid examination: INSPECT neck for goitre (observe while swallowing — thyroid moves with swallowing); PALPATE gland — size (enlarged vs atrophic vs normal), consistency (firm/rubbery = Hashimoto's; hard = malignancy/Riedel's; tender = subacute thyroiditis), nodularity (smooth vs multinodular); AUSCULTATE for bruit (Grave's hyperthyroidism — not hypothyroidism)
Skin: dryness, coarse texture, sallow/yellowish tinge (carotenaemia), loss of outer eyebrow (Queen Anne's sign), non-pitting periorbital and peripheral oedema
Hair: dry, brittle quality; diffuse hair thinning on scalp; lateral eyebrow thinning or loss

Neurological examination: deep tendon reflexes — DELAYED RELAXATION PHASE of ankle jerk (pathognomonic hung-up reflex); cognitive testing (MMSE or MoCA for cognitive impairment); gait and coordination for cerebellar signs; assessment of carpal tunnel — Tinel's and Phalen's signs
Cardiovascular examination: bradycardia; heart sounds (muffled = pericardial effusion); elevated diastolic blood pressure
Respiratory examination: reduced breath sounds at bases (pleural effusion in severe cases)
Eyes: periorbital puffiness; proptosis is NOT present (unlike Grave's ophthalmopathy in hyperthyroidism)
Tongue: macroglossia (enlarged tongue — may indent on teeth)
Voice quality: hoarseness, low pitch, husky quality
Weight and height: calculate BMI; compare with previous measurements if available

diagnostic_tests.description: The single most important and sensitive test for thyroid dysfunction. TSH is produced by the pituitary gland — it reflects the pituitary's assessment of circulating T4/T3 levels over the preceding weeks. In primary hypothyroidism, low T4 triggers a compensatory increase in TSH — a small fall in Free T4 causes a disproportionately large rise in TSH (logarithmic inverse relationship). TSH is the first-line screening test for all forms of suspected thyroid disease except suspected pituitary/hypothalamic disease.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for and confirm hypothyroidism; monitor adequacy of levothyroxine therapy
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal range: 0.4-4.5 mIU/L (varies slightly by laboratory and trimester in pregnancy); Subclinical hypothyroidism: TSH 4.5-10 mIU/L with normal Free T4; Overt hypothyroidism: TSH >10 mIU/L with low Free T4; In pregnancy: TSH target <2.5 mIU/L (first trimester); Monitoring on levothyroxine: target TSH 0.5-2.5 mIU/L
diagnostic_tests.limitations: TSH is NOT elevated in central (pituitary or hypothalamic) hypothyroidism — if suspected, check Free T4 directly; TSH fluctuates slightly with time of day, illness, and recent iodine exposure — retest if borderline; biotin supplements falsely lower TSH (stop biotin 48h before testing)
diagnostic_tests.monitoring_frequency: 4-8 weeks after starting or changing levothyroxine dose; annually once stable on correct dose; every 4-6 weeks during pregnancy

diagnostic_tests.description: Measures the unbound (biologically active) fraction of T4 in serum. Free T4 is the direct measure of thyroid hormone output and reflects actual hormone availability to tissues. In overt primary hypothyroidism, Free T4 is below the reference range. Essential for: confirming overt hypothyroidism (low Free T4 + elevated TSH), diagnosing central hypothyroidism (low Free T4 + low/normal TSH), and monitoring patients with central hypothyroidism (where TSH is unreliable).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm overt hypothyroidism; diagnose central hypothyroidism; guide dosing in pregnancy and central hypothyroidism
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Normal Free T4: typically 10-25 pmol/L (laboratory specific); Low Free T4 with elevated TSH = primary hypothyroidism; Low Free T4 with low/normal TSH = central hypothyroidism

diagnostic_tests.description: Measures the active form of thyroid hormone. T3 is 3-4 times more potent than T4 and is the form that actually binds to nuclear thyroid receptors. Most T3 is derived from peripheral conversion of T4. Free T3 is not routinely measured in primary hypothyroidism diagnosis (TSH and Free T4 sufficient) but is useful in: detecting T3 thyrotoxicosis (hyperthyroidism), monitoring combination T4+T3 therapy, assessing adequacy of T4-to-T3 conversion in patients with residual symptoms on levothyroxine.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Suspected combination T3/T4 therapy monitoring; suspected T3-predominant hyperthyroidism; evaluating persistent symptoms despite normal TSH/Free T4

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Anti-Thyroid Peroxidase Antibodies (Anti-TPO Ab / Anti-Microsomal Ab)
diagnostic_tests.description: Autoantibodies directed against thyroid peroxidase — the enzyme responsible for iodine organification and thyroid hormone synthesis. Anti-TPO antibodies are present in over 90% of patients with Hashimoto's thyroiditis and in 70-80% of patients with Grave's disease. They are the single best test for confirming autoimmune thyroid aetiology and predicting future thyroid failure in subclinical hypothyroidism.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm autoimmune aetiology (Hashimoto's); identify subclinical hypothyroidism patients at highest risk of progression; assess risk in pregnancy (anti-TPO positive in pregnancy increases risk of postpartum thyroiditis and miscarriage)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive: >34 IU/mL (laboratory specific); Strongly positive: >600 IU/mL — high risk of progression; Anti-TPO positive + TSH 4.5-10 = 7-10% annual risk of overt hypothyroidism
diagnostic_tests.note: Anti-TPO does not need routine rechecking once confirmed positive — titre does not guide management changes

diagnostic_tests.description: Autoantibodies directed against thyroglobulin — the protein matrix in which thyroid hormones are stored. Present in 60-80% of Hashimoto's thyroiditis and up to 20-30% of normal population at low titres. Less specific than anti-TPO for Hashimoto's diagnosis. Primarily used in thyroid cancer follow-up — anti-Tg antibodies can interfere with thyroglobulin assay (used to detect cancer recurrence) and must be checked simultaneously.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Support Hashimoto's diagnosis when anti-TPO negative; thyroid cancer follow-up (interference assessment)

diagnostic_tests.description: The first-line imaging modality for the thyroid gland. Provides detailed information on gland size, echogenicity, vascularity, and presence of nodules. In Hashimoto's thyroiditis: heterogeneous, hypoechoic (dark) parenchyma with irregular echotexture and reduced/normal vascularity — these appearances are highly characteristic. Also assesses for nodules (which may need fine-needle aspiration cytology — FNAC), goitre size, and vascular pattern.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm Hashimoto's appearance; characterise goitre; evaluate thyroid nodules; guide FNAC if nodule present; assess gland for Riedel's thyroiditis or infiltrative disease
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Heterogeneous hypoechoic parenchyma + reduced vascularity = highly characteristic of Hashimoto's; Nodule features requiring FNAC: >1 cm solid hypoechoic with microcalcifications, irregular margins, taller-than-wide shape (TI-RADS 4-5)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Lipid Profile (Fasting Cholesterol, LDL, HDL, Triglycerides)
diagnostic_tests.description: Hypothyroidism causes secondary dyslipidaemia — reduced expression of hepatic LDL receptors decreases LDL clearance; impaired lipoprotein lipase activity elevates triglycerides. The lipid profile improves significantly (LDL can fall 15-25%) with levothyroxine replacement — often obviating the need for statin therapy. All patients newly diagnosed with dyslipidaemia should have TSH checked to exclude hypothyroidism as a secondary cause before initiating statin therapy.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Baseline cardiovascular risk assessment; assess secondary dyslipidaemia from hypothyroidism; monitor improvement with treatment
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: LDL elevation and elevated total cholesterol are most characteristic; triglycerides moderately elevated; HDL often low

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Full Blood Count (FBC) / Complete Blood Count
diagnostic_tests.description: Hypothyroidism commonly causes anaemia — usually normochromic normocytic (from reduced erythropoietin and slowed erythropoiesis), but also macrocytic if associated B12 deficiency/pernicious anaemia, or microcytic if iron-deficiency anaemia from menorrhagia. Anaemia may contribute significantly to fatigue.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect hypothyroidism-related anaemia; identify macrocytic anaemia (B12 deficiency — associated autoimmune gastritis); identify iron-deficiency anaemia from menorrhagia
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Hb <120 g/L in women, <130 g/L in men is significant; MCV elevated (macrocytic) = suspect B12/folate deficiency; MCV low (microcytic) = iron deficiency

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Serum Electrolytes, Renal Function, Glucose (U&E, Creatinine, Glucose)
diagnostic_tests.description: Hypothyroidism can cause hyponatraemia (low sodium — from SIADH or decreased renal free water excretion); mild elevation of creatinine (reduced GFR — reversible with treatment); hypoglycaemia tendency (reduced hepatic gluconeogenesis — particularly relevant with concurrent adrenal insufficiency).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect hyponatraemia (which can cause confusion in severe disease); assess renal function; exclude concurrent adrenal insufficiency in secondary hypothyroidism
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Sodium <135 mmol/L = hyponatraemia; may be symptomatic below 128 mmol/L; Creatinine elevation reverses with levothyroxine treatment

diagnostic_tests.description: Significantly elevated CK (creatine kinase) is a characteristic finding in severe hypothyroidism, reflecting myopathic muscle damage. Can be markedly elevated (5-100 times normal). Important to recognise as a hypothyroid sign — CK elevation with myalgia in the absence of statin use or exercise should prompt TSH testing.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Detect hypothyroid myopathy; identify pseudomyopathy (hypothyroidism mimicking myositis or statin myopathy)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: CK >200 U/L with myalgia and no other cause — screen for hypothyroidism; in severe hypothyroidism CK can exceed 10,000 U/L

diagnostic_tests.description: Mild transaminase elevation (AST, ALT) and elevated LDH may occur in hypothyroidism from hepatic metabolic slowing and muscle CK elevation cross-reacting with LDH. LFTs improve with levothyroxine treatment.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Baseline assessment; monitor liver enzymes (relevant if adding T3 therapy); elevated transaminases from hypothyroid hepatopathy

diagnostic_tests.description: Elevated TRH (from hypothyroidism) stimulates pituitary prolactin secretion in addition to TSH — causing hyperprolactinaemia. This is a secondary (not primary) cause of hyperprolactinaemia that resolves with levothyroxine treatment. Important: before investigating for pituitary prolactinoma, always check and treat hypothyroidism first — TSH normalisation resolves the elevated prolactin and may avoid unnecessary pituitary MRI.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess cause of galactorrhoea, menstrual disturbance, and hyperprolactinaemia; distinguish secondary (hypothyroid-driven) from pituitary prolactinoma
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Prolactin >25 mcg/L (women), >20 mcg/L (men) = elevated; Prolactin >100 mcg/L = investigate for pituitary cause even if hypothyroidism present

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Morning Cortisol / Short Synacthen Test (Adrenal Function)
diagnostic_tests.description: CRITICAL when central (secondary/tertiary) hypothyroidism is suspected, or in patients with severe hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine who remain unwell. Adrenal insufficiency (ACTH deficiency) must be excluded or treated BEFORE starting levothyroxine — initiating thyroid hormone without adequate cortisol replacement can precipitate acute adrenal crisis (Addisonian crisis) by increasing cortisol clearance.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude adrenal insufficiency before levothyroxine initiation in suspected central hypothyroidism; assess in myxoedema coma management
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Morning cortisol <100 nmol/L strongly suggests adrenal insufficiency; cortisol >500 nmol/L makes adrenal insufficiency unlikely; Short Synacthen Test (250 mcg IV ACTH) — cortisol peak <500 nmol/L = adrenal insufficiency
diagnostic_tests.note: In myxoedema coma: ALWAYS give IV hydrocortisone empirically before or with levothyroxine to cover potential adrenal insufficiency

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Thyroid Scan (Radionuclide Scintigraphy — Tc-99m or I-123)
diagnostic_tests.description: A nuclear medicine scan that images the thyroid gland's uptake and distribution of radioactive tracer, reflecting functional thyroid tissue. Less commonly used in hypothyroidism diagnosis (ultrasound is preferred) but useful in: (1) identifying ectopic thyroid tissue (lingual thyroid in congenital hypothyroidism); (2) distinguishing Hashimoto's thyroiditis from Grave's disease in the initial hyperthyroid phase; (3) assessing residual thyroid tissue after thyroidectomy or RAI; (4) evaluating 'cold' nodules (low uptake) at higher risk of malignancy.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Congenital hypothyroidism — locate thyroid tissue; postpartum thyroiditis vs Grave's distinction; nodule evaluation
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Hashimoto's/subacute thyroiditis: LOW/patchy uptake; Grave's disease: HIGH diffuse uptake

diagnostic_tests.description: Indicated when central hypothyroidism (pituitary or hypothalamic cause) is suspected — low or inappropriately normal TSH with low Free T4. Pituitary MRI identifies: pituitary adenoma, empty sella syndrome, pituitary apoplexy (haemorrhage), craniopharyngioma, hypothalamic lesions, and signs of Sheehan's syndrome.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose pituitary or hypothalamic pathology causing central hypothyroidism; visual field assessment for suprasellar lesions pressing on optic chiasm
diagnostic_tests.indication: Any patient with low TSH and low Free T4 (central hypothyroidism); deficiency of multiple pituitary hormones; history of pituitary surgery/radiotherapy

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Coeliac Disease Serology (Anti-tTG IgA and Total IgA)
diagnostic_tests.description: Coeliac disease is strongly associated with Hashimoto's autoimmune thyroiditis (shared HLA haplotypes and autoimmune mechanisms). Untreated coeliac disease causes malabsorption of levothyroxine (and selenium and iodine) — making thyroid control more difficult. All patients with Hashimoto's should be screened for coeliac disease, especially if TSH is difficult to control.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for coeliac disease in Hashimoto's patients — associated autoimmune condition; impaired levothyroxine absorption if untreated coeliac
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Anti-tTG IgA >10 times upper limit = strongly positive; confirm with duodenal biopsy (Marsh grade)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC) of Thyroid Nodule
diagnostic_tests.description: Ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration of a thyroid nodule for cytological analysis. NOT routinely performed for hypothyroidism diagnosis — specifically for evaluation of thyroid nodules identified on ultrasound or palpation to determine if malignant. Thyroid cancer can coexist with Hashimoto's thyroiditis.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess malignancy in thyroid nodule >1 cm with high-risk ultrasound features; distinguish benign from malignant nodule
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Bethesda classification: Category I (non-diagnostic) to Category VI (malignant); Category V-VI requires surgical referral
diagnostic_tests.indication: Nodule >1 cm with high-risk ultrasound features (hypoechoic, microcalcifications, irregular margins, lymphadenopathy)

diagnostic_tests.description: Universal newborn screening performed at 5-7 days of life using a small drop of blood from the baby's heel, dried on filter paper. Measures TSH (and Free T4 in some programmes). TSH >40 mIU/L triggers urgent recall, confirmatory blood test, and emergency levothyroxine initiation — before symptoms appear.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Universal screening for congenital hypothyroidism in neonates — to prevent irreversible intellectual disability
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Screening TSH >20 mIU/L requires urgent follow-up; serum TSH >10 mIU/L on confirmation with low T4 = congenital hypothyroidism; treatment must start within first 2 weeks of life for optimal neurodevelopmental outcome

medicines.note: The cornerstone of hypothyroidism treatment is thyroid hormone replacement therapy — most commonly synthetic levothyroxine (T4). Treatment is lifelong in most cases (unless transient cause). The goal is to restore TSH to the normal reference range (0.5-2.5 mIU/L for most patients) and resolve all symptoms. Dose titration requires patience — TSH takes 4-8 weeks to reflect a dose change. All thyroid medications must be managed under physician supervision with regular monitoring. Never adjust dose without blood test guidance.
treatment_principles: 1. Levothyroxine (synthetic T4) is the first-line and standard treatment for all forms of hypothyroidism — endorsed by all major endocrine societies
2. Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach — 30-60 minutes before food (or alternatively at bedtime, at least 3-4 hours after last meal) — food reduces absorption by up to 40%
3. TSH should be checked 4-8 weeks after any dose change — not before, as TSH takes this long to reach a new steady state

4. Treatment targets: TSH 0.5-2.5 mIU/L for most patients; TSH <2.5 mIU/L in pregnancy; TSH 0.1-1.0 mIU/L for thyroid cancer patients on suppressive therapy; TSH 1-4 mIU/L for elderly over 70 (avoid over-treatment)
5. Dose requirements increase in pregnancy — many women need 25-30% dose increase from the very first day of confirmed pregnancy
6. ALWAYS treat adrenal insufficiency BEFORE starting levothyroxine in central hypothyroidism — to prevent precipitating adrenal crisis
7. Never stop levothyroxine abruptly — hypothyroidism will return; if a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered
8. Consistent brand/formulation of levothyroxine is important — switching brands can cause TSH fluctuation due to bioavailability differences; stick to one brand

categories.purpose: Replace the deficient thyroid hormones to restore normal metabolic function, resolve symptoms, and normalise TSH. Levothyroxine (T4) is the standard of care and first-line treatment globally.

medicines.name: Levothyroxine Sodium (Synthetic T4 — L-Thyroxine)
medicines.form: Tablet (12.5 mcg, 25 mcg, 50 mcg, 75 mcg, 88 mcg, 100 mcg, 112 mcg, 125 mcg, 150 mcg, 175 mcg, 200 mcg); IV injection; Oral solution

dosage.standard_starting_dose: Full replacement dose: 1.6 mcg/kg/day (e.g., 70 kg adult = ~112 mcg/day); start at full dose in young, healthy patients with no cardiac risk
dosage.elderly_over_60_or_cardiac_history: Start at 12.5-25 mcg/day; increase by 12.5-25 mcg every 4-6 weeks; slow titration avoids precipitating angina or arrhythmia
dosage.post_total_thyroidectomy: 1.6-2.2 mcg/kg/day (higher in younger patients and cancer patients requiring TSH suppression)
dosage.pregnancy: Increase current dose by 25-30% immediately on confirmed pregnancy; many women need 2 extra doses per week
dosage.children_congenital_hypothyroidism: Neonate: 10-15 mcg/kg/day; 3-12 months: 8-10 mcg/kg/day; 1-5 years: 5-6 mcg/kg/day; 6-12 years: 4-5 mcg/kg/day; reduce toward adult dose during adolescence
dosage.dose_adjustment: Adjust by 12.5-25 mcg increments based on TSH level; recheck TSH 4-8 weeks after every change

medicines.administration: Take on completely empty stomach — 30-60 minutes before breakfast; or at bedtime at least 4 hours after last meal; take with water only (not milk, coffee, or juice); coffee and espresso significantly reduce absorption — take dose first, wait 60 min, then have coffee
medicines.mechanism: Synthetic identical to endogenous T4; converted peripherally to active T3 by selenodeiodinase enzymes in liver, kidney, and other tissues; T3 binds nuclear thyroid hormone receptors regulating gene transcription and metabolic rate
medicines.monitoring: TSH at 4-8 weeks after dose change; annually when stable; every 4-6 weeks throughout pregnancy; Free T4 if central hypothyroidism or ambiguous TSH

drug_interactions.effect: Binds levothyroxine in gut — reduces absorption by 20-40%

drug_interactions.management: Separate by at least 4 hours; critical in pregnancy where both iron and levothyroxine are commonly prescribed

drug_interactions.effect: Reduced gastric acid impairs levothyroxine dissolution and absorption
drug_interactions.management: Take levothyroxine 30-60 min before PPI; consider dose increase if TSH rises after PPI initiation

drug_interactions.effect: Binds levothyroxine in gut — severely reduces absorption

drug_interactions.drug: Soy products (soy milk, tofu, soy protein)
drug_interactions.effect: Soy isoflavones inhibit absorption — particularly relevant in infants on soy formula
drug_interactions.management: Separate by 4 hours; note in infants on soy formula — may need higher levothyroxine dose

drug_interactions.effect: Hepatic enzyme inducers — increase T4 and T3 clearance; may significantly increase levothyroxine requirement
drug_interactions.management: Monitor TSH closely if starting, stopping, or changing doses of these enzyme inducers; may need dose increase of up to 25-50%

drug_interactions.effect: Levothyroxine increases warfarin effect (catabolism of clotting factors) — dose of warfarin may need reduction
drug_interactions.management: Monitor INR closely when initiating levothyroxine or changing doses

drug_interactions.effect: Blocks T4-to-T3 conversion; inhibits thyroid hormone entry into cells; TSH may rise even on correct levothyroxine dose
drug_interactions.management: TSH monitoring every 6 months on amiodarone; dose of levothyroxine may need increase

drug_interactions.effect: High-dose biotin (used for hair/nail growth) interferes with immunoassays — causes FALSELY LOW TSH and FALSELY HIGH T4/T3 on standard laboratory tests
drug_interactions.management: Stop biotin for at least 48-72 hours before any thyroid function blood tests — this is an important and commonly missed source of spurious results

side_effects: Side effects are rare at correct therapeutic doses — symptoms are signs of OVER-TREATMENT (iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis)

Over-treatment signs: palpitations, tremor, anxiety, sweating, diarrhoea, insomnia, weight loss, heat intolerance, tachycardia, atrial fibrillation (particularly dangerous in elderly), osteoporosis (long-term subclinical hyperthyroidism from suppressive doses)
Under-treatment signs: persistence or return of hypothyroid symptoms
Rare true allergic reactions to fillers/dye in specific tablet formulations — switch to different brand or formulation

special_groups.pregnancy: Most critical period — maternal T4 is the only source of fetal thyroid hormone in first trimester (fetal thyroid not functional until weeks 10-12); inadequate replacement risks miscarriage, preeclampsia, preterm birth, and irreversible fetal neurodevelopmental impairment; TSH target <2.5 mIU/L first trimester, <3.0 mIU/L second/third trimester; increase dose by 25-30% immediately on confirmed pregnancy
special_groups.elderly: Start at 12.5-25 mcg; titrate slowly to avoid angina and AF; acceptable TSH target in >75 years may be 1-7 mIU/L (looser target to avoid over-treatment); TSH over 6-7 mIU/L in >80 years: benefit of treatment is less certain
special_groups.cardiac_patients: Start at 12.5 mcg/day; increase by 12.5 mcg every 4-8 weeks; hypothyroidism treatment may unmask angina as cardiac demand increases with metabolic rate; monitor cardiac symptoms closely
special_groups.thyroid_cancer: Suppressive therapy: TSH target 0.1-0.5 mIU/L (low-intermediate risk) or <0.1 mIU/L (high risk disease) to suppress TSH-driven cancer growth; balance against osteoporosis and AF risks of over-treatment

medicines.name: Liothyronine Sodium (Synthetic T3 — L-Triiodothyronine)
medicines.form: Tablet (5 mcg, 25 mcg, 50 mcg); IV injection (for myxoedema coma)
medicines.dosage: Oral (as adjunct): 5-25 mcg/day in divided doses (2-3 times daily due to short half-life); IV myxoedema coma: 5-20 mcg bolus IV, then 2.5-10 mcg every 8 hours
medicines.use_case: 1. IV treatment of myxoedema coma (where T4-to-T3 conversion may be severely impaired); 2. Add-on therapy in patients with persistent symptoms despite optimal TSH on levothyroxine alone — combination T4+T3 therapy; 3. Short-term use before thyroid cancer radioiodine scanning (avoids prolonged levothyroxine withdrawal hypothyroidism)
medicines.mechanism: Directly provides active T3 — does not require conversion from T4; binds nuclear thyroid hormone receptors directly; rapid onset (hours) and short duration of action (half-life ~8 hours vs ~7 days for T4)
side_effects: Palpitations and tachycardia — more pronounced than with levothyroxine due to direct rapid action
Risk of cardiac arrhythmia — use very cautiously in elderly and cardiac patients
Short half-life requires multiple daily dosing — less convenient than once-daily levothyroxine
medicines.note: T3 is NOT recommended as monotherapy for routine hypothyroidism by major endocrine guidelines (BTA, ATA, ETA) — levothyroxine is standard; however, combination T3+T4 therapy may benefit a subset of patients with persistent symptoms on levothyroxine alone; must be supervised by endocrinologist

medicines.name: Desiccated Thyroid Extract (DTE — Natural Thyroid Hormones)
medicines.form: Tablet — standardised extract of porcine (pig) thyroid gland
medicines.composition: Contains both T4 and T3 in fixed 4:1 ratio (by weight); also contains T2, T1, calcitonin, and thyroglobulin
medicines.dosage: Starting dose: 30 mg (equivalent to ~50 mcg levothyroxine); titrate based on clinical response and TSH
medicines.use_case: Some patients with residual symptoms on levothyroxine monotherapy who prefer combined T3+T4; historically first thyroid treatment (1890s) before synthetic hormones developed
medicines.mechanism: Provides both T4 and T3 simultaneously; the fixed T4:T3 ratio (4:1 by weight) provides relatively MORE T3 than human thyroid secretion (actual human ratio ~14:1 T4:T3)
medicines.controversy: Not recommended as first-line by most endocrine guidelines (inconsistent batch-to-batch potency, porcine source, religious concerns, higher T3 content risks cardiac side effects); some patients report subjective preference; evidence for superiority over levothyroxine in RCTs is limited
side_effects: Higher T3 content increases risk of T3-mediated cardiac effects
Batch variability may cause inconsistent TSH control
medicines.note: Discuss with endocrinologist; not routinely recommended but may be considered in select patients with persistent symptoms on optimised levothyroxine after excluding other causes

categories.purpose: Intensive life-saving treatment for myxoedema coma — the most severe presentation of hypothyroidism with mortality up to 60%. Must be managed in ICU.

medicines.name: Intravenous Levothyroxine (IV T4)
medicines.dosage: Loading dose: 200-400 mcg IV bolus (higher dose for younger patients and more severe coma); maintenance: 50-100 mcg IV daily until oral route feasible; transition to oral when patient is conscious and tolerating oral medications
medicines.mechanism: IV route bypasses gut absorption impairment; restores circulating T4 levels; provides substrate for T3 conversion
medicines.note: Always give IV hydrocortisone concurrently or before T4 to prevent adrenal crisis

medicines.name: Intravenous Liothyronine (IV T3) — Alternative or Addition
medicines.dosage: 5-20 mcg IV initial dose; 2.5-10 mcg IV every 8 hours; reduce dose in elderly and patients with ischaemic heart disease (risk of angina and arrhythmia)
medicines.mechanism: Directly provides active T3 without requiring T4-to-T3 conversion — beneficial as deiodinase activity may be severely impaired in critical illness
medicines.note: Some protocols use T4 alone, others T3 alone, and others a combination; T3 has faster onset but higher cardiac risk; consult endocrinology

medicines.name: Intravenous Hydrocortisone
medicines.dosage: 100 mg IV every 8 hours (stress dosing) until adrenal function confirmed adequate; taper and stop when adrenal insufficiency excluded by cortisol testing
medicines.use_case: MANDATORY in myxoedema coma — adrenal insufficiency frequently co-exists (especially if central hypothyroidism or hypopituitarism); levothyroxine increases cortisol clearance — can precipitate life-threatening adrenal crisis if cortisol not supplemented
medicines.mechanism: Replaces cortisol during critical illness; prevents adrenal crisis on initiation of thyroid hormone replacement

categories.purpose: Manage specific symptoms and complications of hypothyroidism while awaiting thyroid hormone replacement to take full effect (typically 6-12 weeks for full symptom resolution).

medicines.name: Statins (for secondary dyslipidaemia)
medicines.dosage: Atorvastatin 10-40 mg once daily; Rosuvastatin 5-20 mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Hypothyroid-related dyslipidaemia — if dyslipidaemia persists after 3-6 months of optimal levothyroxine replacement (TSH normalised) and lipids remain elevated; IMPORTANT: always recheck lipids after 3-6 months of thyroid treatment before prescribing statin — levothyroxine alone reduces LDL by 10-25% in hypothyroid patients
medicines.note: Statins cause myopathy — particularly problematic in hypothyroidism which already causes myopathy and elevated CK; ensure thyroid is optimally treated before attributing myalgia to statin; elevated CK in untreated hypothyroid patient on statin does NOT necessarily indicate statin myopathy

medicines.name: Laxatives (for constipation)
medicines.use_case: Symptomatic constipation while awaiting thyroid hormone effect; typically resolves completely with adequate levothyroxine replacement within weeks
medicines.note: Bulk-forming laxatives (ispaghula) can REDUCE levothyroxine absorption if taken concurrently — separate by at least 4 hours

medicines.name: Antidepressants (for depression — short-term while awaiting thyroid treatment effect)
medicines.note: Hypothyroidism is a reversible cause of depression — all new depression must have TSH measured. Antidepressants should be used cautiously in hypothyroidism until TSH normalised on levothyroxine, as depression may resolve completely with thyroid treatment alone. If antidepressants are prescribed, SSRIs are safest. Do not start antidepressants without confirming thyroid function is normal or optimally treated.

medicines.name: Vitamin D and Calcium Supplementation
medicines.dosage: Vitamin D3: 1000-2000 IU daily (or 60,000 IU weekly for deficiency); Calcium: 500-1000 mg daily
medicines.use_case: Vitamin D deficiency is very common in Hashimoto's autoimmune thyroiditis and may be an associated feature; calcium supplementation if dietary intake is low (but SEPARATE from levothyroxine by minimum 4 hours)
medicines.note: NEVER take calcium supplement within 4 hours of levothyroxine — calcium chelates levothyroxine reducing absorption

medicines.name: Iron Supplementation (for iron-deficiency anaemia from menorrhagia)
medicines.dosage: Ferrous sulphate 200 mg (65 mg elemental iron) twice to three times daily
medicines.use_case: Iron-deficiency anaemia from menorrhagia in premenopausal hypothyroid women; iron deficiency also impairs thyroid hormone synthesis (iron-dependent enzyme thyroperoxidase)
medicines.note: CRITICAL: Separate iron from levothyroxine by at least 4 hours — iron forms insoluble chelate with levothyroxine reducing absorption by up to 50%

categories.purpose: Selenium is an essential micronutrient for thyroid hormone metabolism. Selenoenzyme deiodinases (type 1, 2, 3) catalyse conversion of T4 to active T3 and to inactive reverse T3. Selenium-dependent glutathione peroxidase and thioredoxin reductase protect thyroid cells from oxidative damage during hormone synthesis.

medicines.name: Selenium (as Selenomethionine or Sodium Selenite)
brand_examples: Brazil Nut (natural source — 1 nut contains ~70-90 mcg selenium)
medicines.dosage: 100-200 mcg per day (do not exceed 400 mcg/day — risk of selenosis at high doses); treatment duration: 3-12 months; reassess benefit
medicines.use_case: 1. Hashimoto's thyroiditis — multiple RCTs (CATALYST trial, YEARS study) show selenium 200 mcg/day reduces anti-TPO antibody titres and may slow progression; some studies show improvement in quality of life and thyroid echogenicity on ultrasound. 2. Selenium-deficient patients with hypothyroidism — impaired T4-to-T3 conversion. 3. Autoimmune thyroid disease in pregnancy — reduces postpartum thyroiditis risk in anti-TPO positive women.
medicines.evidence: Meta-analyses: selenium supplementation reduces anti-TPO antibody titres by 30-40% in Hashimoto's; however benefit in terms of preventing progression to overt hypothyroidism or reducing levothyroxine requirement is less established; current NICE and ETA guidelines: can be considered in Hashimoto's but not routinely recommended pending further evidence
side_effects: Selenosis at doses >400 mcg/day: hair loss, nail brittleness, peripheral neuropathy, garlic odour
medicines.food_sources: Brazil nuts (highest food source — 1-3 nuts/day provides adequate selenium); seafood, organ meats, eggs, dairy products

categories.purpose: Correct iodine deficiency in patients with goitre and hypothyroidism from documented iodine deficiency. NOT indicated in autoimmune (Hashimoto's) hypothyroidism — excess iodine can trigger or worsen autoimmune thyroiditis.

medicines.name: Potassium Iodide / Iodised Salt
medicines.form: Iodised salt (20-40 ppm); potassium iodide tablets; iodine-containing multivitamins
medicines.dosage: Adequate iodine intake: 150 mcg/day for adults; 220 mcg/day in pregnancy; 290 mcg/day in lactation; iodised salt provides ~75 mcg iodine per 5g salt (a typical daily salt intake)
medicines.use_case: Prevention and treatment of iodine-deficiency hypothyroidism and goitre in endemic areas; mandatory prenatal vitamin iodine supplementation (150 mcg iodine/day) in women of childbearing age in iodine-deficient regions
medicines.warning: Do NOT give high-dose iodine supplements to patients with Hashimoto's autoimmune thyroiditis — excess iodine triggers increased autoimmune activity, elevates anti-TPO antibodies, and worsens thyroid function. The Wolff-Chaikoff effect: sudden iodine excess transiently blocks thyroid hormone synthesis.
medicines.note: The best population-level prevention is through universal salt iodisation (USI) — WHO and UNICEF global mandate

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Diet plays an important supporting role in thyroid health but should not be considered a replacement for prescribed levothyroxine. Key nutritional principles for hypothyroidism: (1) Ensure adequate iodine and selenium for thyroid hormone synthesis and conversion; (2) Time meals around levothyroxine to optimise absorption; (3) Moderate goitrogen intake sensibly (most healthy people on adequate levothyroxine and iodine do not need to severely restrict goitrogens); (4) Maintain healthy weight through balanced nutrition; (5) Correct associated deficiencies (iron, Vitamin B12, Vitamin D). Do not rely on specific 'thyroid diets' — no specific diet cures hypothyroidism but a balanced, nutrient-sufficient diet supports optimal thyroid function and treatment effectiveness.

essential_nutrients_for_thyroid_function.role: Primary raw material for thyroid hormone synthesis — T3 contains 3 iodine atoms, T4 contains 4. Without adequate iodine, the thyroid cannot produce T3 or T4.
essential_nutrients_for_thyroid_function.recommended_intake: 150 mcg/day adults; 220 mcg/day pregnancy; 290 mcg/day lactation

best_food_sources.content: 20-40 mcg iodine per gram; ~75-150 mcg per 5g (one teaspoon)
best_food_sources.note: The most reliable daily iodine source globally; use iodised salt in cooking (not rock salt, sea salt, or pink Himalayan salt which are not iodised)

best_food_sources.content: Cow's milk: 50-150 mcg iodine per cup; major iodine source in vegetarian Indian diet
best_food_sources.note: Iodine content varies with feed iodine supplementation

best_food_sources.food: Marine fish and seafood (tuna, cod, shrimp, prawns)
best_food_sources.content: Tuna (canned): 17-34 mcg per 85g; cod: 99 mcg per 85g
best_food_sources.note: Excellent iodine source; coastal populations rarely develop iodine deficiency

best_food_sources.content: Highly variable — can contain 11-3,000 mcg per serving
best_food_sources.warning: CAUTION — excessive seaweed/kelp consumption can cause iodine-induced hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism due to extreme iodine variability; kelp supplements are NOT recommended

essential_nutrients_for_thyroid_function.role: Essential cofactor for deiodinase enzymes (converts T4 to active T3) and for glutathione peroxidase (protects thyroid cells from oxidative damage during hormone synthesis). Selenium deficiency impairs T4-to-T3 conversion and worsens autoimmune thyroid inflammation.
essential_nutrients_for_thyroid_function.recommended_intake: 55 mcg/day adults; 60 mcg/day in pregnancy; 70 mcg/day lactation

best_food_sources.content: 1-3 Brazil nuts = 70-270 mcg selenium — the richest single food source
best_food_sources.note: 1-3 nuts per day provides adequate selenium; do not eat large quantities daily (selenosis risk at very high intake)

best_food_sources.food: Fish and seafood (tuna, sardines, shrimp, salmon)
best_food_sources.content: Tuna: 92 mcg per 85g serving — excellent source
1 large egg: ~15-20 mcg selenium; accessible daily source
Selenium content varies with soil selenium content of growing region
~19 mcg per 28g serving; good plant source

essential_nutrients_for_thyroid_function.role: Required for pituitary TSH synthesis and for T3 receptor binding in target cells. Zinc deficiency reduces TSH production and peripheral thyroid hormone action.
best_food_sources: Red meat, especially beef and lamb
Nuts and seeds (pumpkin seeds — highest plant source)
Whole grains (though phytates reduce absorption from plant sources)

essential_nutrients_for_thyroid_function.role: Thyroid peroxidase (TPO) is an iron-dependent enzyme — iron deficiency impairs thyroid hormone synthesis; iron deficiency anaemia is very common in women with hypothyroidism (from menorrhagia and shared autoimmune pathology with pernicious anaemia). Correcting iron deficiency can improve thyroid function.
best_food_sources: Lean red meat (highest bioavailable haem iron)
Dark leafy greens (spinach, methi/fenugreek leaves — non-haem iron; enhance with Vitamin C)
essential_nutrients_for_thyroid_function.note: Avoid taking iron supplements with levothyroxine — separate by minimum 4 hours

essential_nutrients_for_thyroid_function.role: Amino acid precursor to thyroid hormones — iodine is attached to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin to form T3 and T4. Adequate protein intake ensures sufficient tyrosine.
sources: Protein-rich foods: meat, poultry, fish, dairy, eggs, soy, legumes
Dietary deficiency of tyrosine is very rare with adequate protein intake

essential_nutrients_for_thyroid_function.role: Vitamin D receptors are present on thyroid cells; Vitamin D deficiency is associated with increased autoimmunity and higher anti-TPO antibody titres in Hashimoto's thyroiditis; may contribute to thyroid inflammation.
essential_nutrients_for_thyroid_function.recommended_intake: 600-2000 IU/day (or 1500-2000 IU if deficient); target serum 25-OH Vitamin D >75 nmol/L
essential_nutrients_for_thyroid_function.note: Very common deficiency in India (due to indoor lifestyle despite high sunlight) — supplementation often required

recommended_foods.rationale: Hashimoto's thyroiditis involves chronic thyroid inflammation — anti-inflammatory dietary patterns may reduce autoimmune activity

items.benefit: Curcumin — potent anti-inflammatory; inhibits NF-κB inflammatory pathway; reduces inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, TNF-alpha); emerging evidence in autoimmune thyroid disease; widely available in Indian diet
items.frequency: Daily in cooking or turmeric golden milk (with black pepper to enhance curcumin absorption)

items.benefit: Anti-inflammatory gingerols and shogaols; reduces thyroid antibody-associated inflammation; immune modulation
items.frequency: Daily — fresh ginger in cooking, tea, or warm water

items.benefit: Rich in polyphenols and antioxidants; reduce thyroid oxidative stress; amla (Indian gooseberry) is an exceptionally rich source of Vitamin C — supporting iron absorption and thyroid antioxidant defence
