items.frequency: Daily as snack or with breakfast

items.benefit: Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) — anti-inflammatory; reduce thyroid autoimmune activity; selenium (T4-to-T3 conversion); iodine; high-quality protein

items.food: Extra virgin olive oil / Mustard oil (cold-pressed)
items.benefit: Oleocanthal in olive oil has ibuprofen-like anti-inflammatory action; monounsaturated fats support hormonal balance; mustard oil contains omega-3 alpha-linolenic acid
items.frequency: Daily as cooking oil (not for high-heat frying)

recommended_foods.rationale: Emerging evidence supports a gut-thyroid axis — gut microbiome dysbiosis is associated with autoimmune thyroid disease; probiotics may reduce thyroid autoimmunity and improve iodine and selenium absorption; leaky gut may allow thyroid antigen translocation triggering autoimmune response

items.benefit: Probiotics restore gut microbiome; provides iodine (cow's milk); calcium (take 4 hours from levothyroxine); Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium species may reduce gut permeability and autoimmune activity
items.frequency: Daily — plain unsweetened yogurt; best taken at a different time from levothyroxine

items.benefit: Fermented milk with diverse probiotic strains; higher probiotic count than regular yogurt; anti-inflammatory; emerging evidence in autoimmune conditions
Fermented foods with natural probiotics; easily digestible; balanced carbohydrate and protein; staple South Indian food with beneficial fermentation
Traditional fermented probiotic drink; promotes gut health; may support gut-thyroid axis

recommended_foods.rationale: Thyroid hormone is synthesised from tyrosine (amino acid) + iodine; adequate dietary protein ensures sufficient tyrosine substrate; protein also supports muscle mass (reduced by hypothyroid myopathy) and immune function

items.benefit: Complete protein (contains all essential amino acids including tyrosine); selenium (T4-T3 conversion); iodine; Vitamin D; zinc; affordable and versatile
Complete protein; selenium; zinc; low saturated fat; tyrosine-rich
Plant protein; zinc; iron (non-haem — enhance absorption with Vitamin C); fibre (improves constipation); inexpensive and widely available in India
items.frequency: Daily as dal in Indian diet
items.note: Some legumes contain goitrogens — see goitrogen section; cooking greatly reduces goitrogenic activity

recommended_foods.rationale: Constipation is a common hypothyroid symptom — resolves with levothyroxine treatment but dietary fibre supports bowel regularity during transition; however high-fibre diet can slightly reduce levothyroxine absorption if taken concurrently

items.benefit: Soluble fibre — absorbs water, bulks and softens stool; one of the most effective dietary interventions for constipation; widely available in India
items.frequency: 1-2 teaspoons in warm water morning or evening (NOT with levothyroxine — separate by 4 hours)
items.note: Separate isabgol from levothyroxine by at least 4 hours — reduces absorption

items.benefit: Soluble fibre improving constipation; omega-3 fatty acids (anti-inflammatory benefit for Hashimoto's); lignans (phytoestrogens — modest thyroid-supporting effect at normal food doses)
items.frequency: 1-2 tablespoons ground daily in food, yogurt, or water
items.note: Some evidence for anti-thyroid effect at very high supplemental doses in animal studies — normal dietary amounts are safe and beneficial

items.benefit: Soluble fibre (beta-glucan); improves constipation and cholesterol (which is commonly elevated in hypothyroidism); low GI; iron

foods_and_substances_to_manage.category: Goitrogens — Foods That Interfere with Thyroid Hormone Synthesis
foods_and_substances_to_manage.explanation: Goitrogens are substances that impair thyroid hormone synthesis by: (1) inhibiting thyroid peroxidase (TPO) enzyme — reducing iodine organification; (2) blocking iodine uptake into the thyroid. Goitrogens are most relevant in iodine-deficient individuals and in uncooked form. In patients on adequate levothyroxine replacement with sufficient iodine intake, moderate consumption of these foods is SAFE and nutritious. COOKING substantially reduces goitrogenic activity (heat breaks down goitrogenic glucosinolates).

goitrogenic_foods.food: Cruciferous vegetables (broccoli, cabbage, kale, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, radish, kohlrabi, pak choi)
goitrogenic_foods.goitrogen: Glucosinolates (broken down to goitrin and thiocyanates by intestinal bacteria and plant myrosinase enzyme)
goitrogenic_foods.risk: Clinically significant only in raw large quantities in iodine-deficient individuals NOT on levothyroxine; cooking greatly reduces goitrogenic activity
goitrogenic_foods.recommendation: EAT FREELY — these are highly nutritious anti-cancer vegetables; cook them (steam, boil, stir-fry) before eating; moderate raw consumption (a serving of raw coleslaw or salad) is fine for patients on levothyroxine
goitrogenic_foods.myth_busting: The internet-driven extreme avoidance of all cruciferous vegetables in hypothyroidism is NOT supported by evidence for patients on adequate levothyroxine — these vegetables provide vital nutrition including Vitamin C, folate, calcium, and anti-cancer compounds

goitrogenic_foods.food: Soy products (tofu, soy milk, edamame, soy protein isolate)
goitrogenic_foods.risk: More clinically relevant than cruciferous vegetables — soy isoflavones significantly inhibit levothyroxine absorption when taken concurrently; in borderline hypothyroidism, high soy intake may worsen thyroid function
goitrogenic_foods.recommendation: For patients on levothyroxine: consume moderate amounts of soy foods at meal times (not with medication); SEPARATE levothyroxine from soy by minimum 4 hours; infants on soy formula need careful dose adjustment of levothyroxine as soy markedly reduces absorption
goitrogenic_foods.note: Fermented soy (miso, tempeh, natto) may have lower goitrogenic activity due to fermentation breaking down isoflavones

goitrogenic_foods.goitrogen: Contains C-glycosyl flavones and other antithyroid compounds
goitrogenic_foods.risk: Relevant primarily in populations consuming millet as staple grain in iodine-deficient areas (e.g., sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia); cooking reduces but does not eliminate
goitrogenic_foods.recommendation: Regular moderate consumption as part of varied diet is fine for patients on levothyroxine in iodine-sufficient settings; do not make millet the exclusive grain if borderline thyroid function

goitrogenic_foods.goitrogen: Contains cyanogenic glucosides (linamarin) — broken down to thiocyanate which blocks iodine uptake
goitrogenic_foods.risk: Significant in populations relying on poorly-processed cassava as staple food — contributes to endemic goitre and cretinism in iodine-deficient areas
goitrogenic_foods.recommendation: Not a concern for most urban patients consuming occasional cassava as part of varied diet on adequate levothyroxine; important public health consideration in endemic regions

goitrogenic_foods.risk: Very low — moderate consumption is safe for hypothyroid patients on levothyroxine
goitrogenic_foods.recommendation: Peanuts are nutritious (selenium, protein, zinc, monounsaturated fats) — no need to avoid

foods_and_substances_to_manage.category: Levothyroxine Absorption — Food and Drink Timing Rules
foods_and_substances_to_manage.critical_importance: Correct timing of levothyroxine is one of the most important factors in achieving stable TSH control — many cases of 'difficult to control' hypothyroidism resolve with proper medication timing

rules.effect: Reduces levothyroxine absorption by 25-36%; one of the most common causes of elevated TSH in compliant patients
rules.recommendation: Take levothyroxine FIRST on empty stomach with water ONLY; wait minimum 30-60 minutes before having coffee or espresso; caffè latte is worse than black coffee (milk also chelates)

rules.effect: Reduces levothyroxine absorption by 20-40% depending on food composition
rules.recommendation: Take levothyroxine 30-60 minutes before eating, OR at bedtime (≥3-4 hours after last meal); consistent timing is most important — choose one regimen and stick to it

rules.effect: High insoluble fibre can bind levothyroxine — reduces absorption
rules.recommendation: Take levothyroxine well before high-fibre breakfast cereals; separate by at least 1 hour

rules.substance: Calcium-rich foods (milk, yogurt, cheese, calcium-fortified juice)
rules.recommendation: Separate levothyroxine from dairy and calcium-rich foods by minimum 4 hours if possible; for convenience — evening or bedtime dosing avoids morning dairy conflicts

foods_and_substances_to_manage.category: Gluten and Coeliac Disease (Important in Hashimoto's)
foods_and_substances_to_manage.explanation: Coeliac disease (gluten sensitivity causing intestinal damage) is 5-7 times more prevalent in Hashimoto's thyroiditis patients than the general population — shared HLA haplotypes (HLA-DR3, HLA-DQ2/DQ8) and autoimmune mechanisms. Untreated coeliac disease causes: malabsorption of levothyroxine (erratic TSH control), malabsorption of selenium and iodine (worsening thyroid function), and potentiates autoimmune thyroid damage.
recommendation: Screen all Hashimoto's patients for coeliac disease with anti-tTG IgA antibodies and total IgA (to exclude IgA deficiency)
If coeliac disease confirmed: strict gluten-free diet dramatically improves levothyroxine absorption and TSH control; may reduce anti-TPO antibody titres
Non-coeliac gluten sensitivity may also affect some Hashimoto's patients — a 3-month trial of gluten-free diet can be considered if symptoms persist despite optimal TSH

Note: a gluten-free diet is NOT necessary or beneficial for Hashimoto's patients who test negative for coeliac disease; it is unnecessarily restrictive, expensive, and may impair fibre and B-vitamin intake

foods_and_substances_to_manage.effect: Alcohol has a directly toxic effect on thyroid follicular cells; heavy chronic alcohol use suppresses TSH and impairs thyroid function; alcohol disrupts levothyroxine absorption and metabolic consistency; associated with poor medication adherence
foods_and_substances_to_manage.recommendation: Moderate alcohol consumption (within recommended guidelines: <14 units/week UK; avoid in pregnancy) is unlikely to significantly affect thyroid control in patients on stable levothyroxine; heavy drinking worsens thyroid function and medication adherence

sample_meal_plan_for_hypothyroidism.principles: Nutrient-dense, anti-inflammatory, gut-friendly diet; adequate iodine, selenium, and zinc; levothyroxine taken 30-60 minutes before breakfast on empty stomach; consistent daily routine
sample_meal_plan_for_hypothyroidism.early_morning_on_waking: Levothyroxine tablet with a glass of plain water (30-60 minutes before breakfast); do NOT take with milk, coffee, tea, or juice
sample_meal_plan_for_hypothyroidism.breakfast_after_30_to_60_min_wait: Oats porridge with banana, flaxseeds, and a drizzle of honey OR eggs (scrambled/boiled) with whole wheat toast OR idli/dosa with sambar (moderate chutney); cup of chai or coffee AFTER at least 30-60 minutes post-levothyroxine
sample_meal_plan_for_hypothyroidism.mid_morning: Brazil nuts (1-2 nuts — selenium); amla (Indian gooseberry — Vitamin C, antioxidant); or a handful of sunflower seeds
sample_meal_plan_for_hypothyroidism.lunch: Dal (moong or masoor — iron, zinc, protein) + brown rice or roti + cooked vegetables (broccoli, cauliflower, or pumpkin — COOKED to reduce goitrogens) + curd (probiotic, iodine — calcium far away from morning levothyroxine)
sample_meal_plan_for_hypothyroidism.mid_afternoon: Coconut water or herbal tea (green tea in moderation — antioxidants); fruit (banana, papaya, or guava)
sample_meal_plan_for_hypothyroidism.dinner: Fish (salmon, mackerel, rohu — selenium, iodine, omega-3) or chicken curry with minimal heavy spice + mixed cooked vegetables + chapati or light rice; or palak dal (spinach — iron, folate)
sample_meal_plan_for_hypothyroidism.bedtime_optional_alternative_levothyroxi: If taking levothyroxine at bedtime instead — take at least 3-4 hours after dinner; warm turmeric milk (haldi doodh — anti-inflammatory) at least 30 min before bedtime levothyroxine if desired
notes: Always take levothyroxine at a consistent time — same routine every day regardless of breakfast timing
Include iodised salt in cooking (not rock salt or sea salt — not iodised)
Use mustard oil or olive oil for cooking (anti-inflammatory; omega-3 content)
Drink 8-10 glasses of water daily — helps constipation and hydration
Avoid large amounts of raw cruciferous vegetables — prefer cooked; moderate raw consumption is fine
Probiotic foods (curd, buttermilk) support gut-thyroid axis — consume daily

medication_adherence.overview: Consistent, daily levothyroxine use is the single most important lifestyle factor in hypothyroidism management. Poor adherence is the most common cause of elevated TSH and persistent symptoms in compliant-appearing patients.
strategies: Take levothyroxine at the SAME TIME every day — morning on empty stomach, OR consistently at bedtime; choose a time that fits your routine and maintain it
Use pill reminders, phone alarms, or pill dispenser boxes to prevent missed doses
If a dose is missed and remembered the same day — take it; if the next day, skip the missed dose and continue normal schedule (never double dose)
Store levothyroxine at room temperature away from moisture and heat — not in the bathroom (humidity degrades tablets)
Do not run out of medication — maintain a 1-month supply; prescriptions should be renewed before last week of tablets
Stick to the same brand of levothyroxine if possible — switching brands can alter absorption and cause TSH fluctuation; if brand change is necessary, recheck TSH in 4-8 weeks
Never stop levothyroxine without doctor's advice — hypothyroidism will return within weeks

exercise_and_physical_activity.overview: Regular exercise has multiple evidence-based benefits in hypothyroidism: reduces hypothyroid fatigue, supports weight management, improves cardiovascular risk (elevated in hypothyroidism from dyslipidaemia), reduces depression, and may have modest TSH-lowering effects.

recommendations.frequency: 150 minutes moderate intensity per week (30 min, 5 days) or 75 minutes vigorous per week
recommendations.examples: Walking (especially brisk walking — most accessible), cycling, swimming, yoga, Zumba, light jogging
recommendations.benefit: Improves metabolic rate, weight control, cardiovascular health, and mood; reduces fatigue and depression of hypothyroidism

recommendations.examples: Bodyweight exercises (squats, lunges, push-ups), resistance bands, light weights, functional fitness classes
recommendations.benefit: Counteracts hypothyroid myopathy (muscle weakness); increases lean muscle mass and basal metabolic rate; reduces insulin resistance; improves bone density (counteracts over-treatment osteoporosis risk)

recommendations.specific_poses: Sarvangasana (Shoulder Stand) — stimulates thyroid gland; Halasana (Plough) — stimulates thyroid; Matsyasana (Fish Pose) — opens throat, stimulates thyroid; Setubandhasana (Bridge Pose); Ustrasana (Camel Pose); Ujjayi Pranayama — regulates thyroid function; Nadi Shodhana (Alternate Nostril Breathing) — balances autonomic nervous system
recommendations.benefit: Inverted and neck-stretching poses increase blood flow to thyroid gland; pranayama reduces stress and cortisol (cortisol impairs T4-to-T3 conversion); improves flexibility, mood, and energy in hypothyroidism; growing evidence for yoga's benefit in autoimmune conditions

exercise_cautions: Start SLOWLY if newly starting exercise — hypothyroidism causes fatigue and myopathy; excessive exercise before TSH normalises may worsen muscle damage
Monitor heart rate — bradycardia from hypothyroidism may mean maximum heart rate is lower than expected; monitor perceived exertion rather than target heart rate alone
Monitor muscle aching — elevated CK is common in hypothyroidism; strenuous exercise worsens myopathy; defer high-intensity exercise until TSH normalised
Cardiac patients on starting levothyroxine — light walking only until cardiologist clears higher intensity activity
Morning exercise after levothyroxine: wait 30-60 min post-levothyroxine before exercising to avoid absorption impairment from increased gut transit

stress_management.overview: Chronic psychological and physiological stress significantly impairs thyroid function through multiple mechanisms: cortisol from HPA axis activation inhibits T4-to-T3 peripheral conversion; stress promotes autoimmune flares in Hashimoto's; stress affects iodine uptake and thyroid hormone synthesis; psychological stress is a known trigger for autoimmune thyroid disease onset.
strategies: Regular meditation — 10-20 minutes daily; reduces cortisol, supports T4-to-T3 conversion, reduces autoimmune activity
Deep breathing exercises — Pranayama (Ujjayi, Nadi Shodhana); activates parasympathetic nervous system
Adequate sleep — 7-9 hours per night; sleep deprivation suppresses thyroid function and worsens autoimmunity; hypothyroidism itself causes hypersomnia and poor sleep quality — treat both
Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) or counselling — particularly for depression and anxiety associated with hypothyroidism
Regular time in nature, hobbies, social connection — protective against chronic stress
Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) — evidence-based programme; reduces inflammatory cytokines relevant to autoimmune thyroiditis

sleep_hygiene.overview: Sleep disturbances are common in hypothyroidism — both hypersomnia (excessive sleeping) and poor-quality sleep occur. Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is significantly more prevalent due to macroglossia, pharyngeal oedema, and obesity. Treating hypothyroidism usually improves sleep, but OSA may persist and require separate management.
recommendations: Maintain consistent sleep and wake times (circadian rhythm stability supports thyroid axis regulation)
7-9 hours sleep nightly in adults; do not nap excessively during day (interferes with overnight sleep)
Screen for obstructive sleep apnoea — if snoring, witnessed apnoeas, or non-refreshing sleep persist after TSH normalised: polysomnography (sleep study) and consider CPAP therapy

Evening levothyroxine option: some patients achieve better absorption and TSH control with bedtime levothyroxine (taken on empty stomach at least 3-4 hours after dinner) — equivalent or better efficacy than morning dosing and avoids morning absorption issues

smoking_cessation.recommendation: Smoking has complex effects on thyroid: paradoxically may reduce hypothyroid risk but significantly worsens Grave's ophthalmopathy (a thyroid-eye complication) and thyroid cancer outcomes. Smoking cessation recommended universally for overall health benefits. Nicotine replacement therapy does not significantly affect thyroid function.

monitoring_and_follow_up.overview: Hypothyroidism is a lifelong condition requiring regular monitoring. Once stable on correct levothyroxine dose, monitoring requirements are straightforward.
monitoring_schedule: New diagnosis or dose change: TSH at 4-8 weeks (TSH takes this long to stabilise after dose change — testing earlier gives misleading results)
Once TSH stabilised in target range: TSH annually
Pregnancy: TSH every 4-6 weeks throughout pregnancy; immediately increase dose on confirmed pregnancy
After radioiodine therapy or thyroid surgery: TSH at 4-6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, then annually
After starting medications affecting thyroid (amiodarone, lithium, checkpoint inhibitors): TSH at 3 months then every 6 months
After major dose change: TSH at 4-8 weeks; do not retest earlier
In patients >60 years: annual TSH; be alert for signs of over-treatment (palpitations, weight loss, tremor)
Annual lipid profile: dyslipidaemia in hypothyroidism; assess cardiovascular risk
If persistent symptoms despite normal TSH: Free T4 and Free T3; check vitamin B12, D, iron, coeliac serology; consider comorbid depression, sleep apnoea, or fibromyalgia
signs_of_over_treatment_to_monitor: Palpitations, fast heart rate, awareness of heartbeat
New or worsening anxiety, restlessness, or irritability
Increased sweating and heat intolerance (opposite of hypothyroid symptoms)
Atrial fibrillation (especially in elderly) — over-treatment is a major modifiable risk factor for AF
Wrist fracture or spinal fracture — osteoporosis from prolonged over-treatment

hypothyroidism_monitoring_plan.note: Most hypothyroid patients on correct levothyroxine dose are entirely well and require only annual monitoring. This guide helps identify when symptoms indicate dose adjustment or medical attention.

green_zone.criteria: TSH within target range (0.5-2.5 mIU/L for most patients) at last test; no hypothyroid symptoms; no symptoms of over-treatment; taking levothyroxine consistently at same time daily; no new medications that affect absorption; stable weight; good energy
green_zone.action: Continue current levothyroxine dose; annual TSH blood test; annual lipid profile; maintain medication adherence; follow up with GP annually or endocrinologist every 1-2 years

yellow_zone.status: Suboptimal Control — GP Review Within Weeks
yellow_zone.criteria: Return of hypothyroid symptoms (increased fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, low mood, dry skin) despite being on treatment; OR symptoms of over-treatment (palpitations, tremor, anxiety, insomnia, heat intolerance) suggesting TSH too low; TSH out of target range at last test; new medication started that may affect absorption; pregnancy confirmed or planned; dose missed frequently; changed brand of levothyroxine recently
yellow_zone.action: GP review and TSH blood test; review medication timing and absorption factors; dose adjustment as guided by TSH; endocrinology referral if persistent symptoms or difficult TSH control

red_zone.status: URGENT — Seek Medical Attention Same Day or Emergency Department
criteria_immediate: Confusion, disorientation, stupor, or loss of consciousness in a patient with known hypothyroidism — possible myxoedema coma — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES (102/112)
Very low body temperature (feeling extremely cold to touch, shivering uncontrollably, or unable to feel cold) with confusion — hypothermia myxoedema coma
Very slow heart rate (<40 bpm) with dizziness, near-fainting, or chest pain
Rapidly enlarging neck swelling with difficulty breathing or swallowing — possible thyroid malignancy or Riedel's thyroiditis — URGENT REFERRAL
New-onset psychosis or severe acute psychiatric breakdown in a known hypothyroid patient — possible myxoedema madness
Severe hyponatraemia symptoms: seizures, severe confusion, nausea from very low sodium
Myxoedema coma precipitant in severely hypothyroid patient: chest infection, stroke, MI, major surgery, opiate prescription
Severe chest pain in hypothyroid patient starting levothyroxine — may unmask angina — STOP LEVOTHYROXINE and seek emergency care
Sudden severe dyspnoea — possible large pericardial effusion with tamponade
Pregnant woman on levothyroxine with any concerns — contact obstetric team immediately for urgent TSH

complications.description: The most life-threatening complication of untreated or severely undertreated hypothyroidism. Represents extreme hypothyroid decompensation — characterised by hypothermia (<35°C), altered consciousness (stupor to coma), bradycardia, hypoventilation, and hyponatraemia. Most commonly occurs in elderly women with longstanding undiagnosed hypothyroidism after a precipitating event (infection, cold exposure, surgery, or sedative medication). Extremely rare in the era of thyroid function screening but still encountered.
complications.severity: Life-threatening — mortality 20-60% even with optimal ICU treatment
complications.management: ICU admission; IV levothyroxine 200-400 mcg loading dose; IV hydrocortisone 100 mg every 8 hours (must be given before or concurrently with T4); passive rewarming; mechanical ventilation if respiratory failure; IV fluids cautiously (hyponatraemia); treat precipitating cause; continuous cardiac monitoring; expected ICU stay weeks to months

complications.description: Even subclinical hypothyroidism significantly elevates cardiovascular risk through secondary dyslipidaemia — reduced hepatic LDL receptor expression causes elevated total cholesterol, LDL-cholesterol, and triglycerides. Overt hypothyroidism additionally causes diastolic hypertension (peripheral vasoconstriction), bradycardia, reduced cardiac contractility, pericardial effusion, and endothelial dysfunction. Long-term untreated or poorly controlled hypothyroidism accelerates atherosclerosis and increases coronary artery disease, heart failure, and stroke risk.
complications.severity: Moderate to Severe — major cause of excess mortality
complications.management: Optimise levothyroxine (TSH normalisation reduces LDL by 10-25%); recheck lipids after 3-6 months of treatment; statin therapy only if dyslipidaemia persists after optimal thyroid treatment; antihypertensive therapy for persistent diastolic hypertension post-treatment; annual lipid profile and blood pressure monitoring

complications.description: Hypothyroidism disrupts the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis — causing anovulation, oligomenorrhoea, and elevated prolactin (from elevated TRH). Results in treatable infertility and recurrent miscarriage. In pregnancy, maternal hypothyroidism deprives the fetus of essential thyroid hormone in the first trimester (before fetal thyroid is functional) — causing irreversible fetal neurodevelopmental impairment, reduced IQ in offspring, miscarriage, preeclampsia, preterm birth, and placental abruption.
complications.severity: Significant — major treatable cause of infertility and pregnancy loss
complications.management: TSH normalisation (<2.5 mIU/L) before conception; immediate dose increase of 25-30% on confirmed pregnancy; TSH monitoring every 4-6 weeks throughout pregnancy; postpartum dose reassessment

complications.complication: Neuropsychiatric Complications — Depression, Cognitive Impairment, Dementia
complications.description: Thyroid hormone is essential for CNS function — deficiency causes a spectrum of neuropsychiatric manifestations: depression (hypothyroidism is the most important reversible medical cause of depression — all new depression cases must have TSH measured), cognitive impairment and memory loss, psychomotor slowing ('brain fog'), cerebellar ataxia, and in rare severe cases dementia or psychosis ('myxoedema madness'). Prolonged severe hypothyroidism may cause structural brain changes.
complications.severity: Moderate to Severe — significantly affects quality of life and is entirely reversible with thyroid treatment
complications.management: TSH normalisation (most neuropsychiatric symptoms resolve completely with levothyroxine); avoid premature psychiatric labelling without thyroid function testing; antidepressants rarely needed if hypothyroidism adequately treated; allow 3-6 months for full neurological recovery

complications.complication: Peripheral Neuropathy and Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
complications.description: Myxoedematous glycosaminoglycan infiltration compresses peripheral nerves — most commonly the median nerve in the carpal tunnel (carpal tunnel syndrome — bilateral numbness, tingling, and pain in the hands, waking patients at night). Also causes generalised peripheral neuropathy with sensory loss, 'glove and stocking' numbness, and burning dysaesthesias.
complications.management: Levothyroxine treatment typically resolves bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome without surgical intervention over months; nerve conduction studies to confirm diagnosis; wrist splints for symptomatic relief while awaiting treatment effect; surgical carpal tunnel decompression only if no response to 6 months of optimal thyroid treatment

complications.description: An important iatrogenic complication — over-treatment with levothyroxine (suppressed TSH <0.1 mIU/L) causes subclinical thyrotoxicosis which activates osteoclasts, increases bone resorption, and over years significantly reduces bone mineral density (particularly trabecular bone in spine and hip), leading to increased fracture risk. Most relevant in post-menopausal women on suppressive thyroid cancer therapy.
complications.severity: Moderate — preventable with correct dosing and monitoring
complications.management: Avoid unnecessary TSH suppression in benign hypothyroidism — target TSH 0.5-2.5 mIU/L; use lowest TSH-suppressive dose in thyroid cancer patients consistent with recurrence risk; annual DEXA bone density scan in post-menopausal women on suppressive therapy; calcium and Vitamin D supplementation; bisphosphonate therapy if T-score <-2.5

complications.description: Iatrogenic thyrotoxicosis from levothyroxine over-treatment is a significant cause of new-onset atrial fibrillation — particularly in elderly patients. Even subclinical hyperthyroidism (suppressed TSH) triples the risk of AF. AF from thyrotoxicosis increases stroke risk by 3-5 times.
complications.severity: Severe — significant cardiac risk in elderly
complications.management: Careful dose titration in elderly — avoid TSH suppression below 0.5 mIU/L unless cancer indication; annual ECG in elderly on levothyroxine; if AF develops — rate control, anticoagulation assessment (CHA2DS2-VASc score), and levothyroxine dose reduction; AF from thyrotoxicosis may revert to sinus rhythm when TSH normalises

complications.description: Multiple mechanisms cause anaemia in hypothyroidism: (1) Normochromic normocytic anaemia — from reduced erythropoietin and slowed erythropoiesis in bone marrow; (2) Macrocytic anaemia — from associated autoimmune gastritis and pernicious anaemia (B12 deficiency); (3) Iron-deficiency anaemia — from menorrhagia; (4) Mixed anaemia pattern combining all three. Anaemia worsens hypothyroid fatigue significantly.
complications.management: Check FBC, B12, folate, ferritin, and transferrin saturation; correct specific deficiencies (B12 IM injections for pernicious anaemia; oral iron for iron deficiency); levothyroxine treatment reverses the normochromic normocytic component

complications.description: Untreated congenital hypothyroidism causes the most severe complications — irreversible intellectual disability (cretinism), short stature, deafness, and developmental delay. Congenital hypothyroidism is the most common preventable cause of intellectual disability worldwide. With neonatal screening and early treatment, affected children achieve normal neurodevelopment.
complications.severity: Catastrophic if untreated — causes irreversible mental and physical developmental impairment
complications.management: Universal neonatal screening (heel-prick test); levothyroxine started within first 2 weeks of life; lifelong treatment and careful monitoring to maintain Free T4 in upper normal range throughout childhood for optimal neurodevelopment; regular developmental assessment

complications.description: Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is significantly more prevalent in hypothyroidism due to myxoedematous infiltration causing macroglossia (enlarged tongue), pharyngeal oedema, obesity, and reduced respiratory muscle tone. OSA worsens hypothyroid fatigue and cognitive impairment and increases cardiovascular risk.
complications.severity: Moderate — resolves partially with thyroid treatment but often requires independent management
complications.management: Screen for OSA with polysomnography (sleep study) if snoring, witnessed apnoeas, or non-refreshing sleep persist after TSH normalisation; CPAP therapy for moderate-severe OSA; weight loss if obese

complications.complication: Secondary Dyslipidaemia and Non-Alcoholic Fatty Liver Disease (NAFLD)
complications.description: Hypothyroidism-driven dyslipidaemia (elevated LDL, cholesterol, triglycerides) accelerates hepatic lipid accumulation, contributing to non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) — an increasingly recognised hepatic complication. Thyroid hormone receptors in liver regulate lipid metabolism; their absence in hypothyroidism promotes hepatic steatosis.
complications.management: Levothyroxine treatment improves hepatic lipid metabolism; recheck LFTs and lipid profile after 3-6 months of treatment; lifestyle measures (exercise, weight loss) and statin if persistent dyslipidaemia

key_points: Hypothyroidism in pregnancy is critically important — maternal thyroid hormone is the ONLY source of T4 for the fetus during the first trimester (weeks 1-12) before the fetal thyroid becomes functional; inadequate maternal T4 directly impairs fetal brain development

Maternal hypothyroidism (TSH >2.5 mIU/L in first trimester) increases risk of: miscarriage (2-3 fold increased risk), preterm birth, preeclampsia, gestational hypertension, impaired fetal neurodevelopmental outcomes, and reduced child IQ
TSH targets in pregnancy: First trimester: TSH <2.5 mIU/L; Second and Third trimester: TSH <3.0 mIU/L — stricter than non-pregnant targets

Levothyroxine dose requirement increases by 25-50% during pregnancy — physiological demand for thyroid hormone increases due to: increased TBG (thyroid binding globulin) from oestrogen; direct hCG stimulation of TSH receptors (first trimester); increased T4 metabolism; transplacental passage of T4 to fetus
Action when pregnancy is confirmed: IMMEDIATELY increase levothyroxine dose by 25-30% (add 2 extra doses per week is a practical approach); recheck TSH within 4 weeks
TSH monitoring in pregnancy: every 4-6 weeks throughout pregnancy; more frequently if dose changed or TSH abnormal
Postpartum: return to pre-pregnancy dose immediately after delivery; TSH at 6 weeks postpartum; monitor for postpartum thyroiditis in anti-TPO positive women

All pregnant women should take iodine-containing prenatal vitamins — 150-220 mcg iodine/day (NOT kelp or seaweed-derived iodine — variable and unsafe); iodine deficiency even in mildly hypothyroid pregnant women impairs fetal neurological development

Screening: UK NICE guidelines recommend routine TSH screening at booking appointment for women at risk; ATA recommends TSH testing in pregnant women with risk factors; some countries practice universal screening
Anti-TPO positive women in pregnancy: higher risk of hypothyroidism developing during pregnancy and postpartum thyroiditis; more frequent TSH monitoring required
Hashimoto's with current euthyroid state (normal TSH) before pregnancy: TSH monitoring every trimester; start levothyroxine if TSH rises above trimester-specific upper limit
Congenital hypothyroidism: 1 in 2,000-4,000 births; TSH-based neonatal screening has transformed outcomes — treatment within first 2 weeks of life prevents intellectual disability

Neonatal signs (may not be obvious initially): prolonged neonatal jaundice (most common), large fontanelle, macroglossia, hoarse cry, constipation, poor feeding, hypotonia, hypothermia, umbilical hernia
Levothyroxine initiation within 2 weeks of birth is critical — each week of delay results in irreversible intellectual impairment proportional to duration
Starting dose neonates: 10-15 mcg/kg/day; maintain Free T4 in upper half of normal range for age; TSH monitoring every 1-3 months in first year of life
Tablets may be crushed and dissolved in small amount of breast milk or water for feeding to neonates — do NOT dissolve in infant formula or soy formula as absorption impaired
Soy formula significantly reduces levothyroxine absorption — infants on soy formula need higher levothyroxine doses and more frequent monitoring
Children with Down syndrome, Turner syndrome, Type 1 diabetes: annual TSH screening from birth or diagnosis

Acquired hypothyroidism in children (usually Hashimoto's): may present as growth failure, delayed puberty, weight gain, decline in school performance; check TSH in any child with unexplained growth deceleration
Hashimoto's thyroiditis in adolescent girls: increasingly prevalent (1-2%); may fluctuate and initially present as hyperthyroid phase (Hashitoxicosis) before becoming hypothyroid
Puberty effects: hypothyroidism delays puberty; over-treatment can accelerate puberty and advance bone age — TSH monitoring is critical during adolescent growth spurts

Paediatric TSH targets differ from adults — consult age-specific reference ranges; newborn TSH reference range is much higher than adult (normal neonatal TSH may be 10-30 mIU/L in first few days of life before falling)
Prevalence of hypothyroidism increases with age — up to 20% of women over 60 years have elevated TSH; most common endocrine disorder in the elderly
TSH reference range is higher in the elderly — TSH up to 7 mIU/L may be acceptable in patients over 80 years; age-specific reference ranges prevent over-diagnosis and over-treatment

Symptoms of hypothyroidism are easily confused with normal ageing or other conditions in the elderly — fatigue, constipation, cognitive decline, weight gain, bradycardia, and depression all overlap with common geriatric syndromes

Subclinical hypothyroidism in elderly >80 years: treating mild TSH elevation (5-10 mIU/L) in the very elderly is controversial — several studies show no benefit and possible harm (increased AF and fractures); individualised decision based on symptoms and co-morbidities

Overt hypothyroidism in elderly (TSH >10 mIU/L): treat with levothyroxine but START LOW — 12.5-25 mcg/day; increase very slowly every 4-6 weeks by 12.5-25 mcg increments; rapid correction risks precipitating angina, myocardial infarction, or atrial fibrillation

Levothyroxine unmasks angina in elderly — the thyroid's modest lowering of myocardial demand has been 'protecting' undiagnosed coronary artery disease; as metabolic rate normalises, cardiac demand increases and angina may appear; always ask about chest symptoms during dose titration

Myxoedema coma: most commonly occurs in elderly women with undiagnosed hypothyroidism precipitated by infection or cold exposure; highest mortality (>50%); maintain high clinical suspicion in elderly with unexplained hypothermia, bradycardia, and confusion
Polypharmacy in elderly: multiple drug interactions with levothyroxine absorption (calcium, iron, PPIs very common) — careful medication review essential
Cognitive impairment: always check TSH in elderly with new cognitive decline — hypothyroidism is a reversible cause of dementia-like symptoms; TSH testing should be part of routine dementia workup
Hypothyroidism worsens dyslipidaemia and cardiovascular risk — all patients with ischaemic heart disease should have TSH checked
Starting levothyroxine in cardiac patients — begin at 12.5-25 mcg/day; increase by 12.5 mcg every 4-6 weeks; monitor for angina and arrhythmia with each dose increase
Levothyroxine treatment may precipitate or worsen angina — the hypothyroid state has been reducing myocardial oxygen demand; cardiac evaluation before increasing dose in known IHD
Myxoedema coma in cardiac patients — use smaller IV T4 doses to avoid precipitating myocardial ischaemia; T3 is higher risk; close cardiac monitoring

Atrial fibrillation: over-treatment with levothyroxine (TSH suppression) is a major modifiable risk factor for AF in elderly cardiac patients — maintain TSH in 0.5-2.5 mIU/L range; never suppress below 0.5 unless thyroid cancer indication
Heart failure: hypothyroidism reduces cardiac contractility and worsens heart failure; levothyroxine treatment improves cardiac output but dose must be titrated very carefully
Immune checkpoint inhibitors (pembrolizumab, nivolumab, atezolizumab, ipilimumab) used in cancer immunotherapy cause immune-related adverse events (irAEs) — thyroid dysfunction in 20-40% of patients
Most commonly causes destructive thyroiditis with initial hyperthyroid phase followed by hypothyroidism — may be permanent
Thyroid function (TSH and Free T4) should be checked before starting checkpoint inhibitor therapy and before every treatment cycle
Levothyroxine replacement for checkpoint inhibitor-induced hypothyroidism is standard; immunotherapy is usually continued unless severe toxicity

HIV/AIDS patients: hypothyroidism can occur from HIV itself (infiltrative disease, opportunistic infection of thyroid — Pneumocystis, CMV), medications (stavudine, didanosine may affect thyroid), or concomitant autoimmune conditions
Organ transplant recipients on immunosuppressants may have altered levothyroxine requirements — drug interactions with tacrolimus, ciclosporin; check TSH annually

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Influenza can trigger exacerbation of autoimmune thyroiditis (Hashimoto's) through molecular mimicry and immune system activation. Respiratory infections are among the most common precipitants of myxoedema coma in patients with severe uncontrolled hypothyroidism. All patients with autoimmune thyroid disease should receive annual influenza vaccination.

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: PCV15 or PCV20 once; PPSV23 booster after 5 years for high-risk groups
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Pneumonia is the most common precipitant of myxoedema coma in patients with severe hypothyroidism — pneumococcal pneumonia is a major cause. Patients with hypothyroidism on long-term levothyroxine who are over 65 years, immunocompromised (from associated autoimmune conditions or cancer treatment), or have chronic respiratory disease should receive pneumococcal vaccination.
vaccinations_recommended.indication: All adults ≥65 years; younger patients with immunocompromising conditions associated with Hashimoto's (e.g., concurrent Addison's disease, Type 1 diabetes)

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Primary series plus boosters per national schedule
vaccinations_recommended.reason: COVID-19 has been associated with triggering thyroiditis and exacerbating autoimmune thyroid disease including Hashimoto's. SARS-CoV-2 infection can cause transient hyperthyroidism from subacute thyroiditis, followed by hypothyroidism. Patients with hypothyroidism are not at substantially higher risk from COVID-19 itself if well-controlled, but vaccination is recommended universally. Note: COVID-19 vaccines have occasionally triggered thyroiditis post-vaccination (very rare) — monitor TSH in symptomatic patients after vaccination.
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: Follow national vaccination schedule; ensure up-to-date vaccinations

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Hepatitis B is associated with triggering autoimmune thyroid conditions and thyroiditis. Patients with autoimmune thyroid disease (Hashimoto's, Grave's disease) are at increased risk of other autoimmune conditions. Hepatitis B vaccination is recommended for all adults under 60 who are not immune.
vaccinations_recommended.note: Not specific to thyroid disease — part of universal adult vaccination recommendation

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 2 doses if no prior vaccination or documented immunity
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Viral infections (particularly chickenpox/varicella and rubella) can trigger autoimmune thyroiditis flares. Patients with Hashimoto's who are non-immune should ensure they are vaccinated — particularly important before pregnancy (rubella in pregnancy causes congenital rubella syndrome). Note: live vaccines contraindicated in severely immunocompromised patients.
vaccinations_recommended.note: MMR vaccine should be given before pregnancy; check immunity status as part of pre-conception planning

when_to_see_doctor: Symptoms suggestive of hypothyroidism: persistent unexplained fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin and hair, hair loss, depression, cognitive slowing, palpitations, or menstrual irregularities — request TSH blood test
Newly diagnosed hypothyroidism — to discuss starting levothyroxine, appropriate dose, monitoring plan, and what to expect
TSH outside target range on routine blood test — dose adjustment consultation
Pregnancy confirmed or planned — URGENT: immediate TSH check and likely dose increase; do not wait for routine appointment
Recurrent miscarriage or fertility problems — TSH should be measured and optimised
New symptoms on established levothyroxine: possible dose change needed (TSH check) or new comorbidity

Newly prescribed medication known to interact with levothyroxine (calcium, iron, cholestyramine, PPIs, amiodarone, lithium, rifampicin, phenytoin, checkpoint inhibitors) — discuss absorption management and TSH monitoring
Neck lump or goitre changes — new or enlarging goitre, hard nodule, or rapid enlargement requires urgent thyroid evaluation
Persistent symptoms despite normal TSH on levothyroxine — evaluation for combination therapy, selenium, coeliac disease, other contributing causes
Symptoms of over-treatment: palpitations, anxiety, insomnia, weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance — possible TSH too low — check and reduce dose
Postpartum period — TSH at 6 weeks postpartum, especially if anti-TPO positive or had previous postpartum thyroiditis
New diagnosis of autoimmune condition (Type 1 diabetes, coeliac disease, pernicious anaemia, Addison's disease, vitiligo) — request TSH check given high association with Hashimoto's
Family history revealed of thyroid disease — request baseline TSH screening
Annual review if on stable levothyroxine — routine TSH and lipid profile monitoring
emergency_signs: Altered consciousness, stupor, confusion, or coma in a patient with known hypothyroidism — POSSIBLE MYXOEDEMA COMA — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES (102/112/999/911) IMMEDIATELY

Very low body temperature with confusion in an elderly patient — hypothermic myxoedema coma — EMERGENCY; cover patient with blankets (passive warming) while awaiting ambulance — do NOT actively rewarm (can cause vasodilation and cardiovascular collapse)
Heart rate below 40 bpm with syncope, near-fainting, or severe chest pain — severe bradycardia requiring emergency cardiac management
Rapidly worsening dyspnoea in a hypothyroid patient — possible large pericardial effusion causing tamponade, or respiratory failure in myxoedema coma
New acute psychosis or complete psychiatric breakdown in a known hypothyroid patient — possible myxoedema madness — require urgent psychiatric and endocrine evaluation
Sudden severe choking, stridor, or dysphagia with rapidly enlarging neck swelling — possible tracheal or oesophageal compression from thyroid mass or haematoma — EMERGENCY AIRWAY
Pregnant woman with symptoms of severe hypothyroidism (extreme fatigue, confusion, cold) — fetal risk from maternal hypothyroidism is an obstetric emergency
Seizures in a patient with hypothyroidism — possible severe hyponatraemia from SIADH — EMERGENCY SODIUM MANAGEMENT
Severe chest pain on starting or increasing levothyroxine in elderly patient with cardiac history — possible precipitated myocardial ischaemia — STOP LEVOTHYROXINE and seek emergency care immediately

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is hypothyroidism and what does the thyroid gland actually do?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The thyroid gland is a butterfly-shaped gland in the lower front of the neck that produces two hormones — T4 (thyroxine) and T3 (triiodothyronine) — that regulate the speed of virtually all body processes: metabolism, energy production, body temperature, heart rate, digestion, brain function, muscle strength, skin, hair, and reproductive function. Hypothyroidism means the thyroid gland is producing insufficient amounts of these hormones — like having your body's engine running too slowly. Every organ system gradually slows down, resulting in fatigue, weight gain, feeling cold, constipation, dry skin, depression, and brain fog. The vast majority of cases are caused by autoimmune destruction of the thyroid gland (Hashimoto's thyroiditis) or by iodine deficiency globally.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the single best test for hypothyroidism?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) blood test is the single most sensitive, specific, and cost-effective test for diagnosing hypothyroidism. TSH is the pituitary gland's signal to the thyroid — when thyroid hormone falls, the pituitary raises TSH to try to stimulate more production. A small fall in thyroid hormone causes a disproportionately large rise in TSH. TSH is the first-line test for all suspected thyroid disease. A normal TSH (0.4-4.5 mIU/L) essentially rules out significant primary hypothyroidism. If TSH is elevated, a Free T4 test is then added to determine severity and guide treatment.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is hypothyroidism curable, and will I need medication forever?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: For most people, hypothyroidism is a lifelong condition requiring ongoing once-daily levothyroxine (thyroid hormone replacement). However, this is not the same as being 'ill' — on the correct levothyroxine dose, almost all symptoms resolve completely and patients live entirely normal, healthy lives with the same life expectancy as the general population. Certain causes are transient and may resolve: postpartum thyroiditis (returns to normal in 70% of cases within 12 months), drug-induced hypothyroidism (may reverse if causative medication stopped), and subacute thyroiditis. If you are on levothyroxine and feel completely well — that means the treatment is working, not that you no longer need it. Stopping levothyroxine abruptly without medical guidance will cause hypothyroidism to return.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Why does levothyroxine need to be taken on an empty stomach, and what else should I avoid?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Levothyroxine absorption from the gut is affected by many things. Taking it on an empty stomach (30-60 minutes before breakfast) ensures maximum consistent absorption. Key things that reduce absorption and must be separated by at least 4 hours: calcium supplements, iron tablets, antacids containing calcium or magnesium, cholesterol-lowering resins, and soy products. Taking levothyroxine WITH coffee or espresso is one of the most common causes of poor TSH control — coffee significantly reduces absorption. Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs like omeprazole) also reduce absorption and may require a dose increase. The most important principle is consistency — take levothyroxine at the same time every day in the same way.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Are cruciferous vegetables (broccoli, cabbage, kale) and soy really dangerous for hypothyroidism?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: This is one of the most common misconceptions about hypothyroid diet. Cruciferous vegetables contain goitrogens — substances that can impair thyroid hormone synthesis — but only when eaten in very large quantities and in raw form, and primarily in people with iodine deficiency NOT on levothyroxine. For people on levothyroxine with adequate iodine intake, moderate consumption of cooked cruciferous vegetables is entirely safe and nutritionally beneficial (they are rich in anti-cancer compounds, fibre, and vitamins). Cooking substantially destroys goitrogenic compounds. Soy is more relevant — soy foods significantly reduce levothyroxine absorption if taken concurrently; separate levothyroxine from soy by 4 hours. Moderate soy consumption at mealtimes (not with medication) is acceptable.

frequently_asked_questions.question: I'm taking levothyroxine and my TSH is normal, but I still feel tired and unwell. Why?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Persistent symptoms despite a normal TSH on levothyroxine is a real and common concern, and should not be dismissed. Possible reasons include: (1) TSH is 'normal' but not optimal for YOU — some patients feel better with TSH in the lower half of normal (0.5-1.5 mIU/L); (2) Poor levothyroxine absorption — coffee, calcium, iron, PPIs, or inconsistent timing; (3) Coeliac disease reducing absorption — needs testing if Hashimoto's; (4) Associated nutrient deficiencies — iron, Vitamin B12, Vitamin D, selenium deficiency are all very common in Hashimoto's and cause identical fatigue symptoms; (5) Associated conditions — depression, sleep apnoea, fibromyalgia, or anaemia; (6) Suboptimal T4-to-T3 conversion in some patients — discussion with endocrinologist about trial of combination T3+T4 therapy. Never assume 'normal TSH = no problem' — investigate the cause of persistent symptoms.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between Hashimoto's thyroiditis and hypothyroidism?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is the CAUSE — an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks and gradually destroys the thyroid gland. Hypothyroidism is the CONSEQUENCE — the state of insufficient thyroid hormone production that results from this destruction. Most people with Hashimoto's will eventually develop hypothyroidism, but Hashimoto's can exist for years or decades before the thyroid fails sufficiently to cause overt hypothyroidism (this stage is called subclinical hypothyroidism). Hashimoto's is confirmed by positive anti-TPO antibodies and characteristic ultrasound appearance. Hypothyroidism is confirmed by elevated TSH and low Free T4. Having Hashimoto's without overt hypothyroidism still matters — it indicates a higher risk of future hypothyroidism and is associated with other autoimmune conditions.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can hypothyroidism cause depression? Will treating the thyroid cure the depression?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — hypothyroidism is one of the most important reversible medical causes of depression. Thyroid hormones are essential for serotonin synthesis, brain neurotransmitter function, and cerebral glucose metabolism. Deficiency causes a spectrum from low mood and 'brain fog' to frank depressive illness. All patients presenting with new depression should have TSH measured before antidepressants are started. In patients whose depression is caused by hypothyroidism, levothyroxine treatment alone frequently resolves the depression completely within 3-6 months — without antidepressants. However, depression may have multiple causes and co-existing primary depression may coexist with hypothyroidism; in such cases, both should be treated. Never attribute all psychiatric symptoms to hypothyroidism without also assessing for primary mental health conditions.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Is it safe to take levothyroxine during pregnancy? Will my baby be normal?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Not only is levothyroxine safe in pregnancy — it is essential. Inadequate maternal thyroid hormone during pregnancy, especially in the critical first trimester, directly impairs fetal brain development. The fetal thyroid does not become functional until weeks 10-12 of pregnancy — before that, the baby is entirely dependent on the mother's T4. Levothyroxine is the same molecule as the thyroid hormone the mother's thyroid would produce normally — it crosses the placenta in appropriate physiological amounts and is safe for the baby. The dose almost always needs to be increased by 25-50% during pregnancy because the demand for thyroid hormone increases. With proper management — optimised levothyroxine dose and regular TSH monitoring every 4-6 weeks throughout pregnancy — outcomes for both mother and baby are completely normal.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is subclinical hypothyroidism and does it need to be treated?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Subclinical hypothyroidism is defined as a TSH elevated above the upper limit of normal (typically >4.5 mIU/L) with a normal Free T4 — the pituitary is working harder than usual to maintain a normal thyroid hormone output. It is very common (4-10% of adults) and often discovered on routine blood testing. Whether it needs treatment depends on: (1) TSH level — above 10 mIU/L most guidelines recommend treatment regardless of symptoms; (2) Symptoms — if fatigue, weight gain, or other hypothyroid symptoms are present, treatment may help; (3) Anti-TPO antibodies — if positive, higher risk of progression and treatment more likely beneficial; (4) Pregnancy or planning pregnancy — treat if TSH >2.5 mIU/L; (5) Age — in elderly (>75), TSH up to 7 mIU/L may be acceptable without treatment given the risk of over-treatment. Discuss with your doctor — treatment decisions in subclinical hypothyroidism are individualised.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What foods should I definitely eat to support my thyroid?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The most important dietary priorities for thyroid health are: (1) Iodine — use iodised table salt in cooking (not rock salt, sea salt, or Himalayan pink salt which are not iodised); eat dairy products, eggs, and fish regularly; these contain adequate iodine for most people. (2) Selenium — 1-3 Brazil nuts per day provides excellent selenium; seafood, eggs, and chicken are good sources; selenium is essential for converting T4 to active T3. (3) Zinc — lean meat, shellfish, legumes (dal, chana), and pumpkin seeds. (4) Anti-inflammatory foods — turmeric (haldi), ginger, fatty fish, berries, and olive oil may help reduce Hashimoto's autoimmune activity. (5) Probiotics — daily plain yogurt (dahi) and fermented foods support the gut-thyroid axis. (6) Consistent levothyroxine timing is more important than any specific 'thyroid food' — the best dietary advice is a balanced, varied, nutrient-sufficient diet with correct medication timing.

frequently_asked_questions.question: My levothyroxine dose is not working properly — my TSH keeps being abnormal. Why?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: The most common reasons for difficulty controlling TSH on levothyroxine are: (1) Absorption issues — taking medication with coffee, food, calcium, iron, or antacids; the most commonly overlooked cause; (2) Inconsistent timing — varying when the dose is taken causes fluctuating absorption; (3) Medication interactions — PPIs, rifampicin, phenytoin, cholestyramine; (4) Coeliac disease — causes malabsorption in the gut; screen with anti-tTG antibody test in Hashimoto's patients; (5) Biotin supplements — high-dose biotin falsely alters TSH results (stop biotin 48-72 hours before blood test); (6) Brand switching — changing between different brands of levothyroxine changes bioavailability; (7) Newly started medications — amiodarone, lithium, checkpoint inhibitors worsening thyroid function; (8) Pregnancy — dose requirements increase by 25-50%; (9) Non-adherence to medication; (10) Liquid levothyroxine formulation may have better absorption than standard tablets in some patients — discuss with doctor.
